explanation: Combustion of plastics does recover energy but produces CO₂ (greenhouse gas) and potentially toxic gases such as HCl from PVC. Mechanical recycling or chemical recycling are preferable.
correction_tip: Evaluate: burning recovers energy (advantage) but releases CO₂ and toxic gases (disadvantage); recycling is better for sustainability.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Which statement best explains why nylon is classified as a condensation polymer rather than an addition polymer?
option_a: Nylon monomers contain C=C double bonds that open during polymerisation
option_b: Nylon is made from two different monomers each with two functional groups, releasing water as a by-product
option_c: Nylon monomers only contain carbon and hydrogen
option_d: Nylon cannot be recycled
explanation: Nylon (a polyamide) is formed from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid via condensation polymerisation, releasing water. The monomers each have two functional groups.
correction_tip: Condensation polymerisation: bifunctional monomers, small molecule (H₂O) released. No C=C needed.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Thermal cracking differs from catalytic cracking. Which statement is correct?
option_a: Thermal cracking uses a zeolite catalyst and lower temperatures
option_b: Thermal cracking operates at 600–700°C and high pressure, producing mainly alkenes; catalytic cracking uses a zeolite at 400–500°C, producing branched alkanes and aromatic compounds
option_c: Both processes produce identical products
option_d: Catalytic cracking requires no catalyst
explanation: Thermal cracking: 600–700°C, high pressure, mainly alkenes produced. Catalytic cracking: zeolite catalyst, 400–500°C, branched alkanes and aromatic compounds produced.
correction_tip: Thermal: high T, high P, mainly alkenes. Catalytic: zeolite, lower T, branched alkanes + aromatics.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain how bromine water can distinguish between hexane and hex-1-ene, including the chemistry involved.
option_a: Both decolourise bromine water; the rate of reaction distinguishes them
option_b: Hexane turns bromine water blue; hex-1-ene turns it red
option_c: Hex-1-ene decolourises bromine water (orange→colourless) via addition reaction across C=C; hexane does not react as it is saturated
option_d: Hexane decolourises bromine water; hex-1-ene does not because it is unsaturated
explanation: Hex-1-ene has a C=C double bond; bromine adds across it (CH₂=CH... + Br₂ → CHBr–CHBr...) decolourising the solution. Hexane is saturated; it does not react with bromine water in the absence of UV light.
correction_tip: Unsaturated compound + Br₂ → addition product (decolourises). Saturated compound + Br₂ → no reaction (without UV).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A dicarboxylic acid HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH reacts with a diamine H₂N-(CH₂)₆-NH₂. What type of polymer forms and what bond is present in the backbone?
option_a: Polyester; ester bond (-COO-)
option_b: Polyamide; amide bond (-CONH-)
option_c: Addition polymer; no new bond type
option_d: Polypeptide; peptide bond only in living systems
explanation: Dicarboxylic acid + diamine → polyamide (e.g. nylon). The two functional groups react to form amide bonds (-CO-NH-) with elimination of water.
correction_tip: Diamine + dicarboxylic acid → polyamide with amide bonds. Diol + dicarboxylic acid → polyester with ester bonds.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: The equation for fermentation is: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for ethanol production in this reaction. (Mr: C₆H₁₂O₆=180; C₂H₅OH=46; CO₂=44)
explanation: Atom economy = (mass of desired product / total mass of all products) × 100 = (2×46)/(2×46 + 2×44) × 100 = 92/180 × 100 = 51.1%.
correction_tip: Atom economy = (Mr of desired product × moles) / (Mr of all products × moles) × 100.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What colour flame does sodium (Na⁺) produce in a flame test?
option_a: Crimson/red
option_b: Lilac/violet
option_c: Yellow/orange
option_d: Green-blue
explanation: Sodium produces a bright yellow/orange flame. This is very distinctive and can mask other colours.
correction_tip: Na⁺ = yellow/orange (very bright). Li⁺ = crimson. K⁺ = lilac. Cu²⁺ = green-blue.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Which metal ion gives a crimson/red flame colour?
option_a: K⁺
option_b: Na⁺
option_c: Cu²⁺
option_d: Li⁺
explanation: Lithium (Li⁺) gives a crimson/red flame colour.
correction_tip: Li⁺ = crimson. Na⁺ = yellow. K⁺ = lilac. Ca²⁺ = orange-red. Cu²⁺ = green-blue.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What gas is produced when a carbonate is tested with dilute acid?
option_a: Hydrogen
option_b: Oxygen
option_c: Carbon dioxide
option_d: Chlorine
explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acids to produce CO₂: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
correction_tip: Carbonate + acid → salt + water + CO₂. Test CO₂ with limewater (turns milky).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is used to test for oxygen gas in the laboratory?
option_a: Burning splint — makes a squeaky pop
option_b: Glowing splint — relights
option_c: Damp litmus paper — turns blue
option_d: Limewater — turns milky
explanation: Oxygen relights a glowing splint. This is the standard test for O₂.
correction_tip: O₂ = glowing splint relights. H₂ = burning splint squeaky pop. CO₂ = limewater milky.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What colour precipitate forms when Fe³⁺ ions react with NaOH solution?
option_a: Green
option_b: Blue
option_c: Brown/rust
option_d: White
explanation: Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃, which is a brown/rust coloured precipitate.
correction_tip: Fe²⁺ = green precipitate. Fe³⁺ = brown/rust precipitate. Cu²⁺ = blue precipitate.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What does Rf stand for in paper chromatography, and what is its maximum possible value?
option_a: Relative flow; maximum 10
option_b: Retention factor; maximum 1
option_c: Rate factor; maximum 100
option_d: Reaction frequency; maximum 1
explanation: Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent front. As the spot cannot travel further than the solvent, Rf has a maximum value of 1.
correction_tip: Rf = distance of spot / distance of solvent front. Always between 0 and 1.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: How do you test for hydrogen gas?
option_a: Hold a glowing splint near the gas — it relights
option_b: Hold a burning splint near the gas — it makes a squeaky pop
option_c: Bubble the gas through limewater — it turns milky
option_d: Hold damp litmus paper near the gas — it turns blue
explanation: Hydrogen produces a squeaky pop when a burning splint is held near it, as H₂ combusts rapidly.
correction_tip: H₂ = burning splint squeaky pop (H₂ combusts). O₂ = glowing splint relights.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What colour precipitate does Cu²⁺ form with NaOH solution?
option_a: Brown
option_b: Green
option_c: White
option_d: Blue
explanation: Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂, a blue precipitate.
correction_tip: Cu²⁺ = blue precipitate with NaOH. Also gives green-blue flame in flame test.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the test for chlorine gas?
option_a: It turns limewater milky
option_b: It makes a burning splint squeak
option_c: It bleaches damp litmus paper white
option_d: It relights a glowing splint
explanation: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white. Cl₂ is also yellow-green and toxic.
correction_tip: Cl₂ = bleaches damp litmus white (and is yellow-green coloured gas).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A pure substance melts at a single sharp temperature. What does this tell you about its purity?
option_a: Nothing; all substances melt at a single temperature
option_b: It is likely pure; impurities cause melting over a range and lower the melting point
option_c: It contains multiple components
option_d: It has a high molecular mass
explanation: A sharp melting point matching the data book value indicates purity. Impurities lower the melting point and cause melting over a range.
correction_tip: Pure substance = sharp, single MP/BP. Mixture/impure = melts/boils over a range.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What colour does potassium (K⁺) give in a flame test?
option_a: Yellow
option_b: Crimson
option_c: Lilac/violet
option_d: Orange-red
explanation: Potassium gives a lilac/violet flame colour.
correction_tip: K⁺ = lilac. Na⁺ = yellow. Li⁺ = crimson. Ca²⁺ = orange-red.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: In paper chromatography, what is the stationary phase?
option_a: The solvent
option_b: The paper
option_c: The sample
option_d: The pencil line
explanation: In paper chromatography the paper acts as the stationary phase. The solvent is the mobile phase.
correction_tip: Stationary phase = paper (does not move). Mobile phase = solvent (moves up the paper).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What colour precipitate forms when Fe²⁺ ions react with NaOH solution?
option_a: Brown
option_b: Blue
option_c: White
option_d: Green
explanation: Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂, a green precipitate.
correction_tip: Fe²⁺ = green precipitate. Fe³⁺ = brown/rust. Cu²⁺ = blue.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What gas turns damp red litmus paper blue?
option_a: Chlorine
option_b: Hydrogen
option_c: Ammonia
option_d: Carbon dioxide
explanation: Ammonia (NH₃) is alkaline and turns damp red litmus paper blue.
correction_tip: NH₃ = turns damp red litmus blue (alkaline). Cl₂ = bleaches litmus white. CO₂ = turns limewater milky.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: How would you test for sulfate ions (SO₄²⁻) in solution?
option_a: Add AgNO₃ solution — white precipitate forms
option_b: Add BaCl₂ solution acidified with HCl — white precipitate forms
option_c: Add NaOH solution — brown precipitate forms
option_d: Add dilute HCl — effervescence occurs
explanation: SO₄²⁻ + Ba²⁺ → BaSO₄ (white precipitate). The HCl acidification prevents false positives from BaCO₃.
correction_tip: Sulfate test: acidified BaCl₂ → white precipitate BaSO₄ (insoluble in excess acid).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the colour of the precipitate formed when Br⁻ ions react with silver nitrate solution?
option_a: White
option_b: Yellow
option_c: Cream
option_d: Black
explanation: Br⁻ + Ag⁺ → AgBr, a cream precipitate. Cl⁻ gives white AgCl; I⁻ gives yellow AgI.
correction_tip: Cl⁻ = white precipitate AgCl. Br⁻ = cream precipitate AgBr. I⁻ = yellow precipitate AgI.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why can sodium be a problem when performing flame tests on samples that may also contain potassium?
option_a: Sodium burns at too high a temperature
option_b: Sodium produces a bright yellow flame that can mask the lilac colour of potassium
option_c: Sodium and potassium produce the same colour
option_d: Potassium extinguishes the sodium flame
explanation: Sodium produces a very bright yellow/orange flame that can overwhelm and mask the lilac colour of potassium, making K⁺ difficult to identify.
correction_tip: Na⁺ yellow flame is so intense it can mask K⁺ lilac flame — a key limitation of flame tests.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: In paper chromatography, a student measures: spot travelled 4.8 cm; solvent front travelled 8.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value.
correction_tip: Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent front = 4.8/8.0 = 0.6.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: White precipitate forms when NaOH is added to a metal ion solution, but the precipitate dissolves when excess NaOH is added. Which ion is present?
option_a: Ca²⁺
option_b: Mg²⁺
option_c: Al³⁺
option_d: Fe²⁺
explanation: Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric; it dissolves in excess NaOH to form aluminate ions. Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ also give white precipitates but these do NOT dissolve in excess NaOH.
correction_tip: White ppt dissolves in excess NaOH → Al³⁺. White ppt remains in excess → Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: How is the test for NH₄⁺ ions carried out, and what is the positive result?
option_a: Add AgNO₃; cream precipitate forms
option_b: Add dilute HCl; effervescence occurs
option_c: Warm with NaOH solution; ammonia gas produced (turns damp red litmus blue)
option_d: Add BaCl₂; white precipitate forms
explanation: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃(g) + H₂O when warmed with NaOH. The pungent ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue.
correction_tip: NH₄⁺ test: warm with NaOH → NH₃ gas → turns damp red litmus blue.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What advantage does flame emission spectroscopy have over a conventional flame test?
option_a: It only works for sodium
option_b: It produces unique line spectra for each element, is more precise, and can detect multiple metals simultaneously
option_c: It does not require any equipment
option_d: It gives results only as colours visible to the naked eye
explanation: Flame emission spectroscopy produces a unique line spectrum for each element, allowing precise identification and quantitative analysis even when multiple metals are present.
correction_tip: Instrumental flame emission spectroscopy is faster, more precise, and can give quantitative results compared to simple flame tests.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What does a single spot on a chromatogram indicate about a sample?
option_a: The sample is a mixture of at least two compounds
option_b: The sample is pure or contains only one component under those conditions
option_c: The experiment was performed incorrectly
option_d: The compound has a high molecular mass
explanation: A single spot suggests the sample is pure or contains only one component with that Rf value in the chosen solvent.
correction_tip: Single spot = pure (or one component). Multiple spots = mixture. Note: two different compounds could coincidentally have the same Rf.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Which gas decolourises acidified potassium permanganate (KMnO₄)?
option_a: CO₂
option_b: NH₃
option_c: SO₂
option_d: O₂
explanation: SO₂ is a reducing agent that decolourises acidified KMnO₄ (purple → colourless). This can be used as a test for SO₂.
correction_tip: SO₂ decolourises acidified KMnO₄. SO₂ also turns damp blue litmus red (acidic).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the colour of chlorine gas and why is it hazardous?
option_a: Colourless and non-toxic
option_b: Yellow-green and toxic (irritant/corrosive to lungs)
option_c: Brown and explosive
option_d: Blue and oxidising
explanation: Chlorine is a yellow-green gas that is toxic; it irritates and damages the respiratory system even in low concentrations.
correction_tip: Cl₂ = yellow-green, toxic, bleaches litmus. Used as a chemical weapon in WWI.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: In mass spectrometry, what information does the molecular ion peak (M⁺) provide?
option_a: The boiling point of the compound
option_b: The relative molecular mass (Mr) of the compound
option_c: The number of carbon atoms only
option_d: The concentration of the sample
explanation: The molecular ion peak (M⁺, highest m/z peak) in a mass spectrum corresponds to the relative molecular mass (Mr) of the compound.
correction_tip: M⁺ peak (highest m/z) = Mr of compound. Fragmentation pattern identifies the compound.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why must the nichrome wire loop be cleaned between flame tests?
option_a: To prevent the wire from melting
option_b: To prevent contamination from previous samples giving a false colour
option_c: To make the flame hotter
option_d: To remove oxide from the wire surface
explanation: Any residue from a previous sample would contaminate the next test and could give a false or mixed colour, especially if sodium is present.
correction_tip: Clean loop (dip in HCl, heat until no colour) to avoid contamination between tests.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A white precipitate forms with AgNO₃ (acidified with dilute HNO₃) and then dissolves when dilute ammonia is added. Which ion is present?
option_a: I⁻
option_b: Br⁻
option_c: Cl⁻
option_d: SO₄²⁻
explanation: AgCl (white) dissolves in dilute NH₃. AgBr (cream) dissolves only in concentrated NH₃. AgI (yellow) is insoluble in NH₃.
correction_tip: Cl⁻ = white AgCl, dissolves in dilute NH₃. Br⁻ = cream AgBr, dissolves in conc NH₃. I⁻ = yellow AgI, insoluble in NH₃.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What are the advantages of instrumental analysis over traditional chemical tests?
option_a: Cheaper and requires no training
option_b: Faster, more sensitive, more accurate, and can work with very small samples
option_c: Produces coloured precipitates that are easier to see
option_d: No equipment needed
explanation: Instrumental analysis is faster, more sensitive (detects trace amounts), more accurate, and requires much smaller sample sizes than traditional chemical tests.
correction_tip: Instrumental analysis: faster, more sensitive, more accurate, smaller samples, can identify mixtures.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is paper chromatography particularly useful for analysing food dyes?
option_a: It changes the colour of the dyes permanently
option_b: It can separate a mixture of dyes and identify each component by Rf value
option_c: It measures the exact mass of each dye
option_d: It destroys impurities in the food
explanation: Paper chromatography separates mixtures based on differential solubility and can identify components by comparing Rf values with known standards.
correction_tip: Chromatography separates mixtures and identifies components by Rf value comparison with standards.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A student adds NaOH to an unknown solution and observes a white precipitate that does NOT dissolve in excess NaOH. Which ions could be present?
option_a: Al³⁺ only
option_b: Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺
option_c: Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺
option_d: Cu²⁺ or Zn²⁺
explanation: Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ both give white precipitates with NaOH that do NOT dissolve in excess. Al³⁺ also gives white precipitate but it DOES dissolve in excess NaOH.
correction_tip: White ppt, insoluble in excess NaOH → Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺. White ppt dissolves in excess → Al³⁺.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Describe how you would carry out a flame test and state the colour produced by calcium (Ca²⁺).
option_a: Dip paper in solution; hold in flame; Ca²⁺ gives crimson
option_b: Clean nichrome wire loop; dip in sample solution; hold in roaring blue Bunsen flame; Ca²⁺ gives orange-red/brick red
option_c: Dip copper wire in sample; hold in flame; Ca²⁺ gives yellow
option_d: Add acid to sample; hold test tube near flame; Ca²⁺ gives lilac
explanation: Correct procedure: clean nichrome loop, dip in sample, hold in roaring flame. Ca²⁺ gives an orange-red (brick red) flame colour.
correction_tip: Flame test procedure: clean wire → dip in sample → roaring Bunsen flame → observe colour. Ca²⁺ = orange-red/brick red.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain why the acid used to acidify BaCl₂ in the sulfate test must be HCl, not H₂SO₄.
option_a: H₂SO₄ would react with the BaCl₂ to produce an acidic solution
option_b: H₂SO₄ contains SO₄²⁻ ions, which would give a false positive white precipitate
option_c: HCl reacts with BaSO₄ to dissolve it
option_d: H₂SO₄ would neutralise the NaOH
explanation: Adding H₂SO₄ would introduce SO₄²⁻ ions, causing a white precipitate of BaSO₄ regardless of whether the original sample contained sulfate — a false positive.
correction_tip: Use HCl (not H₂SO₄) to acidify BaCl₂ for sulfate test, to avoid introducing SO₄²⁻ ions from the acid.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A mixture of amino acids is separated by paper chromatography. The spots are not visible. What reagent is used to locate them, and what colour do they turn?
option_a: BaCl₂; white spots
option_b: AgNO₃; black spots
option_c: Ninhydrin; purple/brown spots
option_d: Universal indicator; red spots
explanation: Ninhydrin is a locating agent for amino acids. It reacts with amino acids to produce purple/brown spots, making them visible.
correction_tip: Ninhydrin is used to locate amino acids on chromatograms (colourless → purple/brown).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: In GC-MS, what is the role of the gas chromatography (GC) component?
option_a: It identifies each component by its fragmentation pattern
option_b: It separates the components of the mixture based on their interaction with the stationary phase
option_c: It measures the molecular mass of the intact molecule
option_d: It burns the sample to produce ions
explanation: In GC-MS, the GC component separates the mixture into individual components. Each component then enters the mass spectrometer for identification.
correction_tip: GC = separates mixture. MS = identifies each component. Together: GC-MS separates AND identifies.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why must dilute nitric acid (HNO₃) be added before AgNO₃ in the test for halide ions?
option_a: To dissolve the silver nitrate
option_b: To prevent false positives from other ions such as CO₃²⁻ and SO₄²⁻ that also form precipitates with Ag⁺
option_c: To provide H⁺ ions for the reaction
option_d: To oxidise the halide ions
explanation: HNO₃ removes interfering ions such as CO₃²⁻ (which would give Ag₂CO₃, a white precipitate) ensuring any precipitate is due to the halide only.
correction_tip: Acidify with dilute HNO₃ before AgNO₃ to remove interfering anions (CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A sample gives a lilac flame that is difficult to see clearly. What technique can improve visibility?
option_a: Use a larger sample
option_b: View through blue cobalt glass to filter out any yellow sodium contamination
option_c: Use a yellow Bunsen flame
option_d: Add more acid to the sample
explanation: Blue cobalt glass absorbs yellow light from sodium, allowing the lilac colour of potassium to be seen clearly even if sodium contamination is present.
correction_tip: Blue cobalt glass filters out Na⁺ yellow, allowing K⁺ lilac to be seen clearly.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A student performs a chromatography experiment using water as the solvent. The food colouring produces three spots at 2.0 cm, 4.5 cm, and 6.0 cm. The solvent front is at 8.0 cm. Calculate all three Rf values.
correction_tip: Rf = each spot distance ÷ solvent front distance. 2.0/8.0=0.25; 4.5/8.0=0.5625; 6.0/8.0=0.75.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What does the fragmentation pattern in a mass spectrum tell a chemist?
option_a: The colour of the compound
option_b: The boiling point of the compound
option_c: The structural identity of the compound, as each compound produces a unique fragmentation pattern
option_d: Only the molecular mass of the compound
explanation: Each compound fragments in a characteristic way under electron bombardment in the mass spectrometer, producing a unique fragmentation pattern that acts as a "fingerprint" for identification.
correction_tip: Fragmentation pattern = unique fingerprint for identification. M⁺ peak = Mr. Fragment peaks reveal structure.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Describe how to test for CO₂ gas and explain what you would observe in a positive test.
option_a: Pass gas through acidified KMnO₄; it decolourises
option_b: Hold damp red litmus paper near gas; it turns blue
option_c: Pass gas through limewater; it turns cloudy/milky due to formation of CaCO₃
option_d: Hold burning splint near gas; it makes a squeaky pop
explanation: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. The white CaCO₃ precipitate makes the limewater turn milky/cloudy.
correction_tip: CO₂ test: bubble through limewater → turns milky/cloudy (forms CaCO₃ precipitate).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain the difference between mobile phase and stationary phase in chromatography.
option_a: Both phases move at the same speed
option_b: The mobile phase moves through/over the stationary phase; components partition between them based on their relative attraction to each phase
option_c: The stationary phase is always a liquid
option_d: The mobile phase is always a gas
explanation: In chromatography, the mobile phase (solvent/gas) carries components through the stationary phase (paper/column). Components separate based on how strongly they are attracted to each phase.
correction_tip: Mobile phase moves; stationary phase stays still. Components partition between phases → separation occurs.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: An unknown solution is tested: BaCl₂ gives a white precipitate; adding excess HCl does not dissolve it. What ion is confirmed?
option_a: CO₃²⁻
option_b: Cl⁻
option_c: SO₄²⁻
option_d: OH⁻
explanation: BaSO₄ is an insoluble white precipitate that does NOT dissolve in excess HCl. BaCO₃ also gives a white ppt but it dissolves in HCl, releasing CO₂.
correction_tip: White ppt with BaCl₂ + HCl, insoluble in excess acid → SO₄²⁻. BaCO₃ would dissolve in HCl.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups. What information does it provide that mass spectrometry alone cannot?
option_a: The molecular mass of the compound
option_b: The number of isotopes present
option_c: Identification of specific functional groups from characteristic absorption frequencies
option_d: The colour of the compound
explanation: IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups (e.g. O-H, C=O, N-H) from their characteristic absorption frequencies. Mass spectrometry provides Mr and fragmentation pattern but not direct functional group identification.
correction_tip: IR = identifies functional groups. MS = identifies Mr and structure from fragmentation. NMR = hydrogen environments.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A scientist needs to identify metal ions in a sample of river water at very low concentrations. Which technique is most appropriate?
option_a: Paper chromatography
option_b: Flame test with nichrome wire
option_c: Flame emission spectroscopy
option_d: Adding NaOH to form precipitates
explanation: Flame emission spectroscopy is far more sensitive than simple flame tests and can detect and quantify metal ions at very low concentrations. It produces unique line spectra for identification.
correction_tip: For trace metal detection: use instrumental flame emission spectroscopy (more sensitive and quantitative than simple flame tests).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is purity particularly important in pharmaceutical (medicine) chemistry?
option_a: Pure compounds are always cheaper to produce
option_b: Impurities in medicines could be toxic or alter the effectiveness and dosage of the drug
option_c: Pure compounds have a longer shelf life
option_d: Purity only matters for cosmetics, not medicines
explanation: In pharmaceuticals, impurities could be toxic, change the drug's activity, or alter the dose delivered, potentially harming patients.
correction_tip: Pharmaceutical purity is critical: impurities may be toxic or affect drug efficacy and safety.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A student adds NaOH solution to an unknown solution X. A white precipitate forms and dissolves in excess NaOH. When X is warmed with NaOH, a pungent gas turns damp red litmus blue. What ions does X contain?
option_a: Al³⁺ and NH₄⁺
option_b: Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻
option_c: Fe³⁺ and SO₄²⁻
option_d: Mg²⁺ and NH₄⁺
explanation: White precipitate dissolving in excess NaOH indicates Al³⁺ (amphoteric Al(OH)₃). Gas turning red litmus blue on warming with NaOH indicates NH₄⁺ (releases NH₃).
correction_tip: White ppt + dissolves in excess NaOH = Al³⁺. Pungent gas turns red litmus blue on warming = NH₄⁺.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Describe a complete test procedure to identify that a sample contains iron(II) sulfate (FeSO₄).
option_a: Add BaCl₂ only; white precipitate confirms FeSO₄
option_b: Add NaOH → green precipitate (Fe²⁺); add acidified BaCl₂ → white precipitate insoluble in HCl (SO₄²⁻)
option_c: Do a flame test → green flame confirms Fe²⁺; add HCl → effervescence confirms SO₄²⁻
option_d: Add AgNO₃ → cream precipitate; add NaOH → brown precipitate
explanation: FeSO₄ contains Fe²⁺ (green precipitate with NaOH) and SO₄²⁻ (white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂, insoluble in excess HCl). Both tests needed to confirm the compound.
correction_tip: To confirm FeSO₄: test for Fe²⁺ (NaOH → green ppt) AND test for SO₄²⁻ (acidified BaCl₂ → white ppt).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: In paper chromatography, compound A has an Rf of 0.72 in ethanol. A reference standard of the same compound in the same solvent has Rf = 0.72. A second unknown spot has Rf = 0.45. What can be concluded?
option_a: The sample is pure compound A only
option_b: The sample contains compound A and at least one other unknown compound
option_c: The sample contains only the unknown compound with Rf 0.45
option_d: The chromatography experiment was performed incorrectly
explanation: Two spots indicate a mixture. The spot at Rf 0.72 matches compound A. The spot at Rf 0.45 is a different compound. Therefore the sample is a mixture containing compound A plus another substance.
correction_tip: Multiple spots = mixture. Matching Rf to reference = identified component. Different Rf = different compound.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain how GC-MS is used to identify an unknown compound in a forensic sample.
option_a: GC-MS measures the melting point; each compound has a unique melting point in the database
option_b: GC separates mixture components; each component enters MS which fragments it and compares the fragmentation pattern against a library database for identification
option_c: MS first identifies the compound, then GC confirms it by colour
option_d: GC-MS measures the Rf value of each component in the mixture
explanation: In GC-MS: 1) GC separates the mixture. 2) Each separated component enters the mass spectrometer. 3) MS produces a fragmentation pattern. 4) The pattern is matched to a database for identification.
correction_tip: GC-MS: GC separates → MS fragments and identifies using database. Used in forensics, drug testing, environmental analysis.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A sample gives a yellow-orange flame test but no precipitate with NaOH and no precipitate with BaCl₂. What is the most likely identity of the sample?
option_a: Iron(III) sulfate
option_b: Sodium chloride
option_c: Potassium carbonate
option_d: Copper(II) sulfate
explanation: Yellow-orange flame = Na⁺. No precipitate with NaOH (Na⁺ salts are soluble). No precipitate with BaCl₂ (Cl⁻ does not precipitate with Ba²⁺). NaCl fits all observations.
correction_tip: Build up the picture: Na⁺ (yellow flame) + Cl⁻ (no precipitate with BaCl₂, and AgNO₃ would give white ppt) = NaCl.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Assess the limitations of using only paper chromatography to confirm the identity of a compound.
option_a: Paper chromatography has no limitations; it is the most reliable technique
option_b: Rf values can vary with solvent, temperature, and paper; two different compounds can have the same Rf; no structural information is provided
option_c: Paper chromatography can only be used for coloured compounds
option_d: Paper chromatography requires very large sample sizes
explanation: Limitations of paper chromatography: Rf values depend on solvent/conditions; two compounds can coincidentally share an Rf; it gives no structural information; colourless spots need locating agents.
correction_tip: Chromatography limitations: Rf not unique; depends on conditions; no structural info; colourless compounds need locating agents.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A flame emission spectrum for an unknown sample shows a single bright line at the same wavelength as sodium's characteristic emission. What conclusion can and cannot be drawn?
option_a: Can conclude: only sodium is present; Cannot conclude: anything else
option_b: Can conclude: sodium (Na⁺) is present; Cannot conclude: that other metals are absent (they may be present but at undetectable levels or masked)
option_c: Cannot conclude anything from a single line
option_d: Can conclude: the sample is pure sodium metal
explanation: A line matching sodium's wavelength confirms Na⁺ is present. However, other elements could also be present but below detection limits or at wavelengths not analysed. The absence of other lines does not confirm their absence.
correction_tip: Flame emission confirms presence of detected ions. Absence of a signal does not necessarily confirm absence of ion.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A yellow precipitate forms when AgNO₃ (acidified with dilute HNO₃) is added to solution X. Excess ammonia does not dissolve the precipitate. What halide ion is present?
option_a: Cl⁻
option_b: Br⁻
option_c: I⁻
option_d: F⁻
explanation: AgI is a yellow precipitate insoluble in both dilute and concentrated ammonia. AgCl is white and dissolves in dilute NH₃; AgBr is cream and dissolves in concentrated NH₃.
correction_tip: AgCl = white, dissolves in dilute NH₃. AgBr = cream, dissolves in conc NH₃. AgI = yellow, insoluble in NH₃.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain why adding dilute HCl before BaCl₂ is important in the sulfate test, referring to a specific interfering ion.
option_a: HCl dissolves BaSO₄ so the test is negative unless SO₄²⁻ is present in large amounts
option_b: HCl removes CO₃²⁻ ions; BaCO₃ is also a white precipitate, so without acidification a false positive could result from carbonate ions
option_c: HCl converts SO₄²⁻ to a soluble form for the reaction to occur
option_d: HCl oxidises Ba²⁺ so it reacts faster
explanation: Ba²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → BaCO₃ (white precipitate). Adding HCl removes CO₃²⁻ (CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂) before the BaCl₂ is added, preventing a false positive.
correction_tip: Acidify with HCl first to remove CO₃²⁻ and avoid false positive BaCO₃ white precipitate.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: An analyst uses NMR spectroscopy to study a compound. What does NMR spectroscopy reveal about a molecule?
option_a: The number of protons in the nucleus of each atom
option_b: The different chemical environments of hydrogen atoms and how many H atoms are in each environment
option_c: The molecular mass and fragmentation pattern
option_d: The colour and melting point of the compound
explanation: NMR spectroscopy identifies the different chemical environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule and their relative numbers, providing detailed structural information.
correction_tip: NMR: identifies different H atom environments and their ratios → helps determine molecular structure.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A mixture of two miscible liquids with different boiling points is to be separated. Which separation technique is most appropriate and why?
option_a: Filtration; because the liquids have different densities
option_b: Simple distillation; because the liquids have slightly different boiling points and are miscible
option_c: Fractional distillation; because the two liquids have different boiling points and are completely miscible, requiring a fractionating column for effective separation
option_d: Paper chromatography; because the liquids have different Rf values
explanation: Fractional distillation is used for miscible liquids with close boiling points. The fractionating column provides multiple condensation/vaporisation steps for better separation than simple distillation.
correction_tip: Miscible liquids, different BPs → fractional distillation. Immiscible liquids → separating funnel.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: In a flame test, strontium (Sr²⁺) gives a red colour similar to lithium (Li⁺). How can flame emission spectroscopy distinguish between them?
option_a: By using a different colour Bunsen burner
option_b: Each element emits a unique line spectrum at characteristic wavelengths; the spectra of Li⁺ and Sr²⁺ are distinct even if visible colours appear similar
option_c: Sr²⁺ and Li⁺ cannot be distinguished
option_d: By measuring the temperature of the flame
explanation: Flame emission spectroscopy resolves the unique line spectra of each element. Though Li⁺ and Sr²⁺ appear similar red to the naked eye, their line spectra occur at different specific wavelengths, enabling definitive identification.
correction_tip: Instrumental flame emission spectroscopy distinguishes elements by their unique line spectra (specific wavelengths), not just colour.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A compound with Mr = 46 shows a molecular ion peak at m/z = 46 and a fragment at m/z = 45 in its mass spectrum. Suggest an identity and explain the fragment.
option_a: Methane; loss of H gives m/z = 45
option_b: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH); loss of H (mass 1) gives [C₂H₅OH - H]⁺ at m/z = 45
option_c: Propane; loss of CH₃ gives m/z = 45
option_d: Ethanoic acid; loss of OH gives m/z = 45
explanation: Ethanol has Mr = 46 (M⁺ at m/z=46). Loss of one hydrogen gives a fragment at m/z = 45 ([M-1]⁺). This is consistent with ethanol's fragmentation.
correction_tip: Mass spectrum: M⁺ = Mr; fragment m/z = M - (mass of lost group). 46-1=45 → loss of H from ethanol.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Evaluate whether a simple flame test alone is sufficient to confirm the presence of copper in an unknown sample.
option_a: Yes; the blue-green flame colour is unique to copper and no further testing is needed
option_b: No; while a blue-green flame suggests Cu²⁺, other compounds or contamination could produce similar colours; confirmatory testing (e.g. NaOH precipitate or instrumental analysis) is needed
option_c: No; flame tests cannot detect copper at all
option_d: Yes; instrumental analysis would give the same result so the flame test is sufficient
explanation: A blue-green flame is indicative of Cu²⁺ but is not conclusive alone. Contamination or other compounds could give similar colours. Confirmatory tests (blue precipitate with NaOH, or flame emission spectroscopy) are required for certainty.
correction_tip: Evaluate: flame tests are indicative but not conclusive. Always confirm with a second test or instrumental method.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A pharmaceutical company wants to check the purity of a newly synthesised drug compound. Describe TWO methods they could use and explain what a pure compound would show in each.
option_a: Flame test (no colour change) and chromatography (multiple spots)
option_b: Melting point (sharp single value matching literature) and thin-layer chromatography (single spot with Rf matching pure reference)
option_c: Mixing with acid (no reaction) and burning (clean blue flame)
option_d: Adding NaOH (no precipitate) and testing with limewater (stays clear)
explanation: A pure drug shows: 1) A sharp melting point matching the literature value (impurities lower and broaden the MP). 2) A single spot on TLC with Rf matching the pure reference compound.
correction_tip: Purity tests: 1) Sharp MP = pure. 2) Single TLC spot with correct Rf = pure. Impurities cause range MP and extra spots.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is homeostasis?
option_a: The production of hormones by glands
option_b: The maintenance of a stable internal environment
option_c: The transmission of nerve impulses
option_d: The breakdown of glucose in respiration
explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function.
correction_tip: Homeostasis = maintaining stable internal conditions (e.g. temperature, blood glucose, water levels).

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the normal core body temperature in humans?
explanation: Normal human core body temperature is approximately 37°C, which is optimal for enzyme activity.
correction_tip: 37°C is the optimum temperature for human enzymes. Deviating from this can denature enzymes.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the name of the gap between two neurones?
option_a: Axon
option_b: Synapse
option_c: Receptor
option_d: Effector
explanation: A synapse is the junction between two neurones where chemical neurotransmitters transfer signals.
correction_tip: Synapse = gap between neurones. Signals cross via neurotransmitter chemicals, not electrical signals.

subject: Biology
question_text: Which part of the nervous system coordinates responses to stimuli?
option_a: Effectors
option_b: Receptors
option_c: Central nervous system
option_d: Peripheral nerves only
explanation: The central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) processes information from receptors and coordinates responses.
correction_tip: CNS = brain + spinal cord. It processes stimuli and sends instructions to effectors.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is a reflex arc?
option_a: A voluntary response to a stimulus
option_b: An automatic, rapid response to a stimulus
option_c: A hormone-based response
option_d: A slow deliberate action
explanation: A reflex arc is an automatic, involuntary and rapid response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought.
correction_tip: Reflex arcs are fast and automatic — they do not involve conscious thought (the brain is bypassed).

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the correct order of a reflex arc?
option_a: Effector → CNS → receptor
option_b: Receptor → CNS → effector
option_c: Stimulus → effector → receptor
option_d: CNS → receptor → effector
explanation: Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS → motor neurone → effector → response.
correction_tip: Remember: Receptor detects, sensory carries in, CNS processes, motor carries out, effector acts.

subject: Biology
question_text: Where is insulin produced?
option_a: Liver
option_b: Kidneys
option_c: Pancreas
option_d: Pituitary gland
explanation: Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
correction_tip: Pancreas produces both insulin (lowers blood glucose) and glucagon (raises blood glucose).

subject: Biology
question_text: What does insulin do to blood glucose levels?
option_a: Raises them
option_b: Lowers them
option_c: Has no effect
option_d: Converts glucose to fat only
explanation: Insulin lowers blood glucose by stimulating cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert glucose to glycogen.
correction_tip: Insulin lowers blood glucose. Glucagon raises it. They work antagonistically.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is Type 1 diabetes?
option_a: The body does not respond to insulin
option_b: The pancreas does not produce enough insulin
option_c: Too much insulin is produced
option_d: Glucagon is overproduced
explanation: In Type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the beta cells, so the pancreas cannot produce insulin.
correction_tip: Type 1 = no insulin produced (pancreas faulty). Type 2 = cells do not respond to insulin.

subject: Biology
question_text: Which gland produces adrenaline?
option_a: Pancreas
option_b: Pituitary
option_c: Adrenal glands
option_d: Thyroid
explanation: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands, which sit above the kidneys.
correction_tip: Adrenal glands (above kidneys) produce adrenaline — the "fight or flight" hormone.

subject: Biology
question_text: Which hormone stimulates the release of an egg during the menstrual cycle?
option_a: Oestrogen
option_b: Progesterone
option_c: LH
option_d: FSH
explanation: A surge in LH (luteinising hormone) triggers ovulation — the release of a mature egg.
correction_tip: LH surge → ovulation. FSH stimulates egg maturation. Oestrogen rebuilds uterus lining.

subject: Biology
question_text: What does FSH do during the menstrual cycle?
option_a: Triggers ovulation
option_b: Maintains uterus lining
option_c: Stimulates eggs to mature in the ovary
option_d: Causes menstruation
explanation: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) stimulates the development and maturation of follicles in the ovaries.
correction_tip: FSH = follicle stimulating hormone → eggs mature. LH = triggers release of egg (ovulation).

subject: Biology
question_text: Which organ is mainly responsible for regulating blood water content?
option_a: Liver
option_b: Lungs
option_c: Kidneys
option_d: Skin
explanation: The kidneys filter blood and regulate water, salt, and urea levels through a process called osmoregulation.
correction_tip: Kidneys control water balance via osmoregulation. ADH controls how much water is reabsorbed.

subject: Biology
question_text: What hormone controls water reabsorption in the kidneys?
option_a: Insulin
option_b: ADH
option_c: Adrenaline
option_d: Glucagon
explanation: ADH (anti-diuretic hormone) is released by the pituitary gland and causes the kidneys to reabsorb more water, producing concentrated urine.
correction_tip: ADH = anti-diuretic hormone. More ADH = more water reabsorbed = small, concentrated urine.

subject: Biology
question_text: What type of neurone carries impulses FROM the CNS to effectors?
option_a: Sensory neurone
option_b: Relay neurone
option_c: Motor neurone
option_d: Receptor neurone
explanation: Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS (brain/spinal cord) to effectors (muscles and glands).
correction_tip: Motor = movement → carries signals away from CNS. Sensory = carries signals TO CNS.

subject: Biology
question_text: What happens to blood vessels in the skin when body temperature rises too high?
option_a: They constrict
option_b: They dilate
option_c: They disappear
option_d: They produce sweat
explanation: Vasodilation occurs — blood vessels near the skin surface widen, allowing more blood to flow near the surface and lose heat.
correction_tip: Hot → vasodilation (widen) → more heat lost. Cold → vasoconstriction (narrow) → less heat lost.

subject: Biology
question_text: How does a nerve impulse cross a synapse?
option_a: By electrical current jumping across the gap
option_b: By neurotransmitter chemicals diffusing across the gap
option_c: By the axon extending across the gap
option_d: By direct contact between neurones
explanation: When an impulse reaches a synapse, neurotransmitters are released from vesicles, diffuse across the synaptic cleft, and bind to receptors on the next neurone.
correction_tip: Synapses use chemicals (neurotransmitters) not electricity. The signal is chemical → electrical again.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why are reflexes faster than voluntary responses?
option_a: Reflexes use faster chemicals
option_b: Reflexes bypass the brain, going through the spinal cord
option_c: Reflexes travel along shorter motor neurones
option_d: Reflexes do not use neurones
explanation: In a spinal reflex, the signal is processed in the spinal cord rather than the brain, reducing response time.
correction_tip: Reflex arcs use the spinal cord as the relay, not the brain → shorter pathway → faster response.

subject: Biology
question_text: How does insulin lower blood glucose?
option_a: By stimulating the kidneys to excrete glucose in urine
option_b: By stimulating cells to absorb glucose and the liver to convert it to glycogen
option_c: By breaking down glycogen into glucose
option_d: By preventing glucose from entering the blood
explanation: Insulin stimulates body cells (especially liver and muscle) to take up glucose from the blood and converts it to glycogen for storage.
correction_tip: Insulin lowers blood glucose: cells take up glucose AND liver converts excess to glycogen (storage form).

subject: Biology
question_text: What does glucagon do to blood glucose?
option_a: Lowers it by stimulating glycogen synthesis
option_b: Has no effect on blood glucose
option_c: Raises it by stimulating glycogen breakdown in the liver
option_d: Raises it by producing more glucose in the kidneys
explanation: Glucagon is released when blood glucose is too low. It stimulates the liver to break down glycogen back into glucose (glycogenolysis).
correction_tip: Glucagon = raises glucose. Stimulates liver to break down glycogen → glucose → released into blood.

subject: Biology
question_text: How is Type 2 diabetes different from Type 1?
option_a: Type 2 involves no insulin at all; Type 1 involves partial insulin
option_b: Type 2 occurs when body cells become resistant to insulin; Type 1 when insulin is not produced
option_c: Type 2 only affects children; Type 1 affects adults
option_d: Type 2 is caused by an infection; Type 1 by poor diet
explanation: In Type 2 diabetes, cells lose sensitivity to insulin, so blood glucose remains high even though insulin may be present.
correction_tip: Type 1 = no insulin produced. Type 2 = cells don't respond to insulin (insulin resistance), linked to obesity.

subject: Biology
question_text: Which hormones are used in the contraceptive pill?
option_a: FSH and LH
option_b: Oestrogen and progesterone
option_c: Testosterone and adrenaline
option_d: ADH and insulin
explanation: The combined contraceptive pill contains oestrogen and progesterone, which inhibit FSH production and prevent egg maturation.
correction_tip: Contraceptive pill = oestrogen + progesterone → inhibit FSH → no egg development → no pregnancy.

subject: Biology
question_text: How does IVF use hormones to increase the chance of pregnancy?
option_a: Progesterone is given to trigger ovulation
option_b: FSH is given to stimulate production of multiple eggs
option_c: Adrenaline is given to prepare the uterus
option_d: LH is suppressed to prevent ovulation
explanation: In IVF, FSH is given in large doses to stimulate the ovaries to produce multiple eggs, which are then collected and fertilised outside the body.
correction_tip: IVF uses FSH to superovulate (produce many eggs). Eggs are collected, fertilised externally, then embryos placed in uterus.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the role of the hypothalamus in temperature regulation?
option_a: It produces sweat
option_b: It monitors and regulates core body temperature
option_c: It controls blood glucose
option_d: It stimulates muscles to shiver
explanation: The hypothalamus acts as the thermostat of the body — it detects changes in blood temperature and coordinates responses.
correction_tip: Hypothalamus = body's thermostat. It detects temperature change and sends signals to skin/muscles.

subject: Biology
question_text: When body temperature drops, what response helps generate heat?
option_a: Sweating
option_b: Vasodilation
option_c: Shivering
option_d: Hair lying flat
explanation: Shivering involves rapid muscle contractions which release heat energy through respiration, helping to raise body temperature.
correction_tip: Cold → shivering (muscle contraction generates heat), vasoconstriction (reduce heat loss), hair standing up (trap air).

subject: Biology
question_text: What effect does adrenaline have on the body?
option_a: Slows heart rate and digestion
option_b: Increases heart rate, dilates pupils, redirects blood to muscles
option_c: Lowers blood pressure
option_d: Decreases blood glucose
explanation: Adrenaline prepares the body for "fight or flight" — it increases heart rate, dilates pupils, and increases blood flow to muscles.
correction_tip: Adrenaline = fight or flight. Heart rate up, pupils dilate, blood to muscles, glucose released.

subject: Biology
question_text: What are effectors?
option_a: Cells that detect stimuli
option_b: Neurones that carry impulses to the brain
option_c: Muscles or glands that produce a response
option_d: Cells in the hypothalamus
explanation: Effectors are the muscles or glands that respond to nerve impulses or hormonal signals from the CNS.
correction_tip: Receptors detect stimuli. Effectors (muscles/glands) carry out the response.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is negative feedback in homeostasis?
option_a: A system that amplifies changes away from the normal level
option_b: A system that reverses changes to return to the normal set point
option_c: A system that maintains constant hormone levels without adjustment
option_d: A system where changes continue once started
explanation: Negative feedback is the mechanism by which a change in the body is detected and corrections are made to reverse the change back towards the set point.
correction_tip: Negative feedback: deviation detected → response opposes the change → returns to normal.

subject: Biology
question_text: What role does oestrogen play in the menstrual cycle?
option_a: Triggers ovulation directly
option_b: Repairs and thickens the uterus lining and stimulates LH surge
option_c: Prevents implantation
option_d: Stimulates FSH release throughout the cycle
explanation: Oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining after menstruation and causes a surge in LH which triggers ovulation.
correction_tip: Oestrogen thickens uterus lining and (at high levels) triggers LH surge → ovulation.

subject: Biology
question_text: What does progesterone do after ovulation?
option_a: Causes the uterus lining to break down
option_b: Maintains the uterus lining if fertilisation occurs
option_c: Stimulates another egg to mature
option_d: Inhibits progesterone production
explanation: After ovulation, the corpus luteum produces progesterone which maintains the thickened uterus lining for implantation.
correction_tip: Progesterone = maintains uterus lining (after ovulation/during pregnancy). If no pregnancy, levels drop → menstruation.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the difference between nervous and hormonal control?
option_a: Nervous is slower and longer-lasting; hormonal is faster and short-lived
option_b: Nervous is faster and short-lived; hormonal is slower and longer-lasting
option_c: Both act at exactly the same speed
option_d: Nervous uses blood; hormonal uses neurones
explanation: Nerve impulses travel quickly but effects are short-lived. Hormones travel in blood, act more slowly but effects last longer.
correction_tip: Nervous: fast, short-lived, precise target. Hormonal: slow, long-lasting, widespread effect.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the role of the relay neurone in a reflex arc?
option_a: Detects the stimulus
option_b: Carries the impulse to the effector
option_c: Connects the sensory and motor neurones in the CNS
option_d: Releases neurotransmitters at the muscle
explanation: Relay neurones (interneurones) are located in the CNS and connect sensory neurones to motor neurones.
correction_tip: Relay neurone = connects sensory to motor in the spinal cord/brain. It is in the CNS.

subject: Biology
question_text: A student touches a hot surface and instantly withdraws their hand. Which pathway correctly describes this reflex?
option_a: Receptor → motor neurone → relay neurone → sensory neurone → effector
option_b: Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in spinal cord → motor neurone → effector
option_c: Receptor → brain → spinal cord → motor neurone → effector
option_d: Receptor → relay neurone → sensory neurone → brain → effector
explanation: The correct reflex arc is: receptor (skin) → sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector (muscle).
correction_tip: Reflex arc bypasses the brain — the spinal cord processes the reflex. Order: receptor → sensory → relay → motor → effector.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain why blood glucose must be kept within narrow limits.
option_a: Too much glucose causes dehydration; too little causes cells to produce more ATP than needed
option_b: Too much glucose causes osmotic damage to cells; too little means cells cannot respire properly
option_c: Blood glucose affects only kidney function, which must be stable
option_d: Glucose regulates temperature, which must stay at exactly 37°C
explanation: High blood glucose causes water to leave cells by osmosis (dehydration); low blood glucose means cells lack fuel for respiration and cannot function.
correction_tip: High glucose: osmotic problems (water moves out of cells). Low glucose: not enough fuel for cellular respiration.

subject: Biology
question_text: A patient's blood glucose rises to 9 mmol/L. Which sequence of events returns it to normal?
option_a: Pancreas releases glucagon → liver breaks down glycogen → blood glucose rises
option_b: Pancreas releases insulin → cells take up glucose, liver converts glucose to glycogen → blood glucose falls
option_c: Adrenal glands release adrenaline → muscles use more glucose → blood glucose falls
option_d: Hypothalamus releases ADH → kidneys retain glucose → blood glucose falls
explanation: High blood glucose → pancreas (beta cells) secretes insulin → cells take up glucose and liver converts it to glycogen → blood glucose returns to set point.
correction_tip: High glucose → insulin released → glucose taken up + converted to glycogen → glucose levels fall back to normal.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why does vigorous exercise lower blood glucose even without insulin?
option_a: Exercise causes insulin to be released from the muscles
option_b: Muscle cells take up and respire more glucose during exercise
option_c: Exercise causes the liver to store more glycogen
option_d: Glucagon is released, lowering glucose
explanation: During exercise, muscle cells increase their rate of aerobic/anaerobic respiration, using more glucose. This lowers blood glucose independently of insulin.
correction_tip: Exercise increases glucose uptake by muscles for respiration — blood glucose drops. This is why diabetics must monitor glucose during exercise.

subject: Biology
question_text: A woman takes a high-dose FSH injection as part of IVF treatment. What is the purpose of this, and what is a risk?
option_a: Purpose: trigger ovulation. Risk: no eggs are released
option_b: Purpose: stimulate multiple eggs to mature. Risk: ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
option_c: Purpose: maintain uterus lining. Risk: early menstruation
option_d: Purpose: prevent ovulation until the right time. Risk: hormonal imbalance
explanation: High FSH doses cause superovulation (multiple eggs mature). A risk is ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), where ovaries become enlarged and painful.
correction_tip: IVF FSH: purpose = many eggs mature (superovulation). Risk = OHSS — ovaries over-respond. Also multiple births if multiple embryos implant.

subject: Biology
question_text: How does the skin reduce heat loss when body temperature falls?
option_a: Sweat glands increase secretion; blood vessels dilate
option_b: Sweat glands reduce secretion; vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near skin; hairs erect trapping air
option_c: Muscles relax to reduce heat production; vasodilation occurs
option_d: The hypothalamus stops monitoring temperature
explanation: When cold: sweat glands stop sweating, blood vessels constrict (less heat lost from skin), hairs stand up (trap insulating air layer).
correction_tip: Cold response: no sweating, vasoconstriction, hairs erect (goosebumps). All reduce heat loss. Shivering also generates heat.

subject: Biology
question_text: How do drugs like caffeine and alcohol affect synapses?
option_a: They destroy neurotransmitters permanently
option_b: They can mimic, block or alter the release of neurotransmitters
option_c: They increase the number of synapses in the brain
option_d: They speed up impulse transmission along axons
explanation: Many drugs act at synapses by mimicking neurotransmitters (e.g. some painkillers), blocking receptors, or altering neurotransmitter release.
correction_tip: Drugs affect synapses: can mimic neurotransmitters (bind to receptors), block them, or affect their release/breakdown.

subject: Biology
question_text: A person dehydrates on a hot day. How does negative feedback restore water balance?
option_a: Less ADH is released; kidneys produce more dilute urine
option_b: More ADH is released; kidneys reabsorb more water; less urine is produced
option_c: More insulin is released; cells absorb more water
option_d: Less glucagon is released; liver releases water into the blood
explanation: Dehydration → blood water potential drops → hypothalamus detects this → pituitary releases more ADH → kidneys reabsorb more water → urine is concentrated.
correction_tip: Dehydrated: ADH increases → kidneys reabsorb more water → small, concentrated urine. Well-hydrated: less ADH → dilute, large-volume urine.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why does the menstrual cycle restart if fertilisation does not occur?
option_a: LH levels remain high maintaining the corpus luteum
option_b: Progesterone and oestrogen levels fall as the corpus luteum degenerates, causing the uterus lining to shed
option_c: FSH levels fall permanently, stopping the cycle
option_d: The uterus lining thickens until it breaks under its own weight
explanation: Without fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone and oestrogen fall, and the uterus lining breaks down (menstruation). Low levels then allow FSH to rise again.
correction_tip: No fertilisation → corpus luteum degenerates → progesterone/oestrogen fall → uterus lining sheds → menstruation → cycle restarts.

subject: Biology
question_text: Evaluate the use of insulin injections versus dietary control in managing Type 1 diabetes.
option_a: Diet alone can cure Type 1 diabetes; insulin injections are only for emergencies
option_b: Insulin injections are essential for Type 1 because the pancreas cannot produce insulin; diet can help but cannot replace insulin
option_c: Type 1 diabetics only need injections when blood glucose is extremely high
option_d: Dietary control is always more effective than insulin injections
explanation: Type 1 diabetics cannot produce insulin at all, so injections are essential. Dietary management helps control glucose intake but cannot replace the need for insulin.
correction_tip: Type 1 = no insulin produced → must inject. Type 2 can sometimes be managed with diet/exercise/weight loss, but Type 1 always requires insulin.

subject: Biology
question_text: A student's pupil reflex is tested. Shining a light in the eye causes the pupil to constrict. Which muscles are involved?
option_a: Longitudinal (radial) muscles contract
option_b: Circular muscles contract
option_c: Both circular and longitudinal contract simultaneously
option_d: No muscles are involved; the iris simply expands
explanation: When light is bright, circular muscles in the iris contract, making the pupil smaller (constrict) to protect the retina.
correction_tip: Bright light: circular muscles contract → pupil constricts. Dim light: radial/longitudinal muscles contract → pupil dilates.

subject: Biology
question_text: How does the kidney produce urine through ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption?
option_a: Blood is fully passed into the urine; useful substances are then added back
option_b: Small molecules are filtered from blood into the tubule; useful substances (glucose, some water) are selectively reabsorbed back
option_c: Only urea is filtered; all other substances remain in blood
option_d: Water is filtered out completely and urea is reabsorbed
explanation: In the glomerulus, high pressure forces small molecules (glucose, urea, water, ions) into Bowman's capsule. As filtrate travels down the tubule, glucose and needed water/ions are reabsorbed. Urea remains and is excreted.
correction_tip: Kidney: ultrafiltration (all small molecules out of blood) → selective reabsorption (glucose + needed water back in) → urea/excess water left as urine.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why might clomifene therapy be used to treat infertility?
option_a: It directly produces eggs outside the body
option_b: It blocks oestrogen receptors in the brain, causing FSH and LH levels to rise, stimulating ovulation
option_c: It provides artificial progesterone to maintain the uterus lining
option_d: It prevents the contraceptive pill's hormones from working
explanation: Clomifene blocks oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary, so the brain thinks oestrogen is low, increasing FSH/LH release and stimulating ovulation.
correction_tip: Clomifene → blocks oestrogen feedback → brain releases more FSH/LH → ovulation stimulated. Used when ovulation is irregular or absent.

subject: Biology
question_text: Compare the speed and specificity of hormonal versus nervous communication.
option_a: Hormones: fast and specific to one cell type. Nerves: slow and widespread
option_b: Hormones: slow (travel in blood), widespread effect. Nerves: fast (electrical), specific target
option_c: Both travel at the same speed, but hormones are more specific
option_d: Hormones travel through neurones; nerves use blood
explanation: Nerves carry electrical impulses rapidly to specific cells. Hormones travel slowly via blood and can affect many different target organs.
correction_tip: Nerves = fast electrical signals, precise. Hormones = slow (bloodstream), longer-lasting, less precise target.

subject: Biology
question_text: A person with diabetes insipidus cannot produce ADH. What would you expect in their urine?
option_a: Very concentrated, small volume urine
option_b: Very dilute, large volume urine
option_c: Urine containing glucose
option_d: Urine with very high urea concentration
explanation: Without ADH, the kidneys cannot reabsorb water, so large volumes of very dilute urine are produced (diabetes insipidus).
correction_tip: No ADH → kidneys don't reabsorb water → large volumes of dilute urine. Not the same as diabetes mellitus (blood sugar disorder).

subject: Biology
question_text: A student claims: "Reflexes are uncontrollable — once a stimulus occurs, you cannot stop the reflex response." Is this correct?
option_a: Yes — reflexes are entirely automatic with no override possible
option_b: Mostly true, but higher brain centres can sometimes inhibit reflexes with practice or conscious effort
option_c: Completely wrong — all reflexes can be consciously stopped instantly
option_d: Only true for spinal reflexes; cranial reflexes are always controllable
explanation: While reflexes are largely automatic, the brain can sometimes modulate them — for example, trained performers can suppress blinking or withdrawal reflexes. However, very fast reflexes (like the knee-jerk) are very difficult to override.
correction_tip: Reflexes are mainly automatic but not completely uncontrollable. Brain can send inhibitory signals — e.g. doctors can examine knee jerk by distracting patient.

subject: Biology
question_text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using an artificial pancreas to treat Type 1 diabetes compared to regular insulin injections.
option_a: Artificial pancreas is always better — no disadvantages
option_b: Artificial pancreas automatically monitors glucose and delivers insulin continuously (advantage) but is expensive and has technical failure risks (disadvantages)
option_c: Injections are always superior because they allow precise control
option_d: Neither method works — Type 1 can only be managed by diet
explanation: An artificial pancreas uses continuous glucose monitoring with an insulin pump for automatic delivery, reducing hypo/hyperglycaemia risk. However, it is costly, requires maintenance, and device failure is a risk.
correction_tip: Artificial pancreas: pros = automatic, continuous, reduces human error. Cons = cost, technical risk, not a cure.

subject: Biology
question_text: A researcher finds that inhibiting progesterone production causes implantation to fail. Explain why.
option_a: Progesterone stimulates ovulation, so without it no egg is available
option_b: Progesterone maintains the uterus lining thickness; without it the lining thins and cannot support the embryo
option_c: Progesterone produces FSH, which is needed for implantation
option_d: Progesterone inhibits LH, and LH is needed for implantation
explanation: Progesterone is essential for maintaining the thickened uterus lining (endometrium). Without it, the lining breaks down and an embryo cannot implant.
correction_tip: Progesterone maintains endometrium. No progesterone → lining breaks down → embryo cannot implant. This is how some contraceptive methods work.

subject: Biology
question_text: A marathon runner has high blood glucose at the start of the race. Explain the changes in blood glucose and hormones over 3 hours of running.
option_a: Blood glucose rises throughout as the body digests food faster during exercise
option_b: Blood glucose falls as muscles use glucose for respiration; glucagon is released to break down glycogen; blood glucose is maintained
option_c: Insulin is released throughout to manage glucose; blood glucose stays perfectly stable
option_d: Glucagon lowers blood glucose throughout and no insulin is needed
explanation: Muscles use glucose rapidly → blood glucose falls → glucagon released → glycogen broken down to glucose → blood glucose stabilised. As glycogen depletes, glucose may drop further.
correction_tip: Exercise: muscles use glucose → blood glucose drops → glucagon → glycogenolysis. Insulin not prominent here. Glycogen stores may run out after ~90 min in marathon.

subject: Biology
question_text: Some toxins block acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. Predict the effect on the body.
option_a: Muscles would contract continuously
option_b: Nerve impulses would reach the junction but muscles could not contract, causing paralysis
option_c: More neurotransmitter would be released to compensate
option_d: Reflexes would speed up due to less resistance
explanation: Blocking acetylcholine receptors prevents the neurotransmitter from binding to muscle cells, so no contraction signal is received → muscle paralysis.
correction_tip: Neuromuscular junction: nerve releases acetylcholine → muscle receptor binds → muscle contracts. Block receptors → no signal received → paralysis (e.g. curare arrow poison).

subject: Biology
question_text: A patient has a tumour in the islets of Langerhans producing excess insulin. Predict and explain the symptoms.
option_a: The patient would have persistently high blood glucose (hyperglycaemia)
option_b: The patient would have persistently low blood glucose (hypoglycaemia) causing confusion and unconsciousness
option_c: The patient would produce no glucagon
option_d: The patient would develop Type 2 diabetes
explanation: Excess insulin → cells continuously take up glucose and liver converts it to glycogen → blood glucose too low → brain cells starve → confusion, seizures, unconsciousness.
correction_tip: Excess insulin = hypoglycaemia. Brain depends on glucose — low blood glucose causes neurological symptoms.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain why the contraceptive pill can cause ethical concerns in some religious or cultural contexts, while still being scientifically effective.
option_a: The pill reduces fertility permanently, which is the main ethical concern
option_b: The pill prevents ovulation and may prevent implantation; some consider preventing implantation to be morally equivalent to ending a potential life
option_c: The pill has no ethical concerns — it is universally accepted
option_d: The pill increases fertility, which some groups object to
explanation: The pill prevents ovulation (main mechanism) but may also alter the uterus lining, potentially preventing implantation. Those who believe life begins at fertilisation may object to this.
correction_tip: Pill = mainly prevents ovulation (no egg = no fertilisation). Also thins endometrium. Some object as this could prevent implantation of a fertilised egg.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why is it important for homeostasis to use negative feedback rather than positive feedback?
option_a: Positive feedback is not found in living organisms
option_b: Negative feedback reverses deviations, maintaining stable conditions; positive feedback would amplify deviations, causing dangerous instability
option_c: Negative feedback is faster than positive feedback
option_d: Positive feedback can only lower variables, not raise them
explanation: Negative feedback counters changes, restoring equilibrium. Positive feedback amplifies changes (e.g. blood clotting — used in specific rapid responses) and would be dangerous if applied to temperature or blood glucose.
correction_tip: Negative feedback = stabilising (corrects deviation). Positive feedback = amplifying (used in childbirth contractions, clotting) — not suitable for homeostasis.

subject: Biology
question_text: Heroin binds to opioid receptors in the brain, mimicking natural endorphins. Explain why this leads to addiction.
option_a: Heroin destroys synapses permanently, forcing the brain to build new ones
option_b: Heroin floods receptors with a stronger signal than natural endorphins, causing euphoria; the brain down-regulates natural endorphin production, creating dependency
option_c: Heroin increases the number of synapses, making users feel better
option_d: Heroin blocks pain receptors directly in the spinal cord only
explanation: Heroin mimics endorphins at opioid receptors, causing intense pleasure. Over time the brain produces fewer natural endorphins and the person needs heroin just to feel normal.
correction_tip: Addiction: drug mimics neurotransmitter → brain reduces natural production → dependency (needs drug to function normally).

subject: Biology
question_text: In a warm environment, a person's core temperature starts to rise. Describe the complete sequence of thermoregulation.
option_a: Hypothalamus detects drop → sends signals → sweating stops → blood vessels constrict
option_b: Thermoreceptors detect rise → hypothalamus processes signal → sweat glands produce sweat (evaporates, cooling skin) → vasodilation increases blood flow to skin → heat lost by radiation
option_c: Pituitary gland detects heat → releases ADH → kidneys produce more urine → body cools
option_d: Muscles shiver to generate cold energy that counteracts the heat
explanation: Rising temperature → thermoreceptors → hypothalamus → sweat glands active (evaporative cooling) + vasodilation (more heat radiated from skin surface) → temperature falls back to 37°C.
correction_tip: Hot: sweating (evaporation cools) + vasodilation (more blood near skin, more heat radiated). Hairs lie flat. Negative feedback restores 37°C.

subject: Biology
question_text: Evaluate the ethical issues surrounding IVF, including the fate of unused embryos.
option_a: There are no ethical issues — IVF is purely beneficial
option_b: IVF helps infertile couples but raises issues about unused embryo destruction, multiple births, and embryo selection; some believe embryos have full moral status from fertilisation
option_c: IVF is ethically problematic only because it uses hormones
option_d: Unused embryos are always used for other couples, so there is no ethical concern
explanation: IVF benefits infertile couples but involves creating multiple embryos, some of which may be discarded or frozen. Beliefs about when life begins create ethical debate. Selection can also raise eugenics concerns.
correction_tip: IVF ethics: unused embryo fate (destroyed/frozen/donated), multiple births risk, cost, embryo selection (designer babies debate), religious views on life's start.

subject: Biology
question_text: A drug inhibits the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in the synapse. Predict and explain the effect on nerve signalling.
option_a: Impulse transmission would stop as acetylcholine cannot bind to receptors
option_b: Acetylcholine would accumulate in the synapse, continuously stimulating receptors, causing prolonged muscle contraction or overactivity
option_c: The presynaptic neurone would release less acetylcholine to compensate
option_d: The post-synaptic neurone would produce its own acetylcholine instead
explanation: Normally the enzyme acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh to stop the signal. Inhibiting it → ACh builds up → receptor stays activated → continuous muscle stimulation (e.g. organophosphate nerve agent effect).
correction_tip: ACh broken down by acetylcholinesterase after signal. Block this enzyme → ACh stays → receptor continuously stimulated → prolonged contraction/overactivation.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why might someone with uncontrolled Type 1 diabetes have glucose in their urine, even though glucose is usually reabsorbed?
option_a: The kidneys have no mechanism for reabsorbing glucose
option_b: Blood glucose is so high that it exceeds the kidney's maximum reabsorption capacity (renal threshold), so excess glucose passes into urine
option_c: Insulin causes the kidneys to excrete glucose directly
option_d: High glucose destroys the kidney tubule cells
explanation: The kidney has a maximum rate of glucose reabsorption (renal threshold ≈ 10 mmol/L). If blood glucose exceeds this, glucose remains in the filtrate and appears in urine (glycosuria).
correction_tip: Kidney renal threshold: normally all glucose reabsorbed. If blood glucose too high → exceeds reabsorption capacity → glucose in urine (glycosuria) → first sign of undiagnosed diabetes.

subject: Biology
question_text: Compare the pupil reflex with a spinal reflex. What is different about where they are processed?
option_a: Both are processed in the spinal cord
option_b: The pupil reflex is a cranial reflex processed in the brainstem; spinal reflexes are processed in the spinal cord
option_c: The pupil reflex requires conscious thought; spinal reflexes do not
option_d: Both are processed in the hypothalamus
explanation: The pupil reflex is coordinated in the brainstem (a cranial reflex), while spinal reflexes (like withdrawing from pain) are processed in the spinal cord. Both are involuntary.
correction_tip: Spinal reflexes: processed in spinal cord. Cranial reflexes (pupil, blinking): processed in brainstem. Both are involuntary and fast.

subject: Biology
question_text: A student says: "Homeostasis only involves temperature control." Evaluate this statement.
option_a: Correct — temperature is the only variable regulated by homeostasis
option_b: Incorrect — homeostasis also regulates blood glucose, water balance, blood CO₂/O₂, pH, and ion concentrations
option_c: Partially correct — temperature and blood glucose are regulated but not water or ions
option_d: Correct, because all other systems are controlled by the nervous system, not homeostasis
explanation: Homeostasis regulates many variables including temperature, blood glucose, water balance, blood pH, CO₂ and O₂ levels, and ion concentrations — all to maintain a stable internal environment.
correction_tip: Homeostasis covers: temperature (37°C), blood glucose (4-8 mmol/L), water balance (osmoregulation), blood pH, CO₂/O₂ levels, ion concentrations.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain how negative feedback controls oestrogen levels during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle.
option_a: High oestrogen stimulates more FSH release, continuing egg development indefinitely
option_b: Rising oestrogen initially inhibits FSH (negative feedback), preventing more follicles developing; but very high oestrogen near ovulation switches to positive feedback, triggering LH surge
option_c: FSH controls oestrogen levels directly with no feedback
option_d: Progesterone is the main hormone that controls oestrogen via negative feedback
explanation: Moderate oestrogen inhibits FSH (negative feedback — ensures only one dominant follicle). Very high oestrogen near ovulation switches to positive feedback, triggering the LH surge that causes ovulation.
correction_tip: Menstrual cycle uses both feedbacks: moderate oestrogen → negative feedback on FSH. Very high oestrogen → positive feedback → LH surge → ovulation. Rare example of positive feedback in homeostasis.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is a gene?
option_a: A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
option_b: The complete set of chromosomes in a cell
option_c: A type of cell in the nucleus
option_d: A single strand of RNA
explanation: A gene is a section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for the production of a specific protein, which determines a characteristic.
correction_tip: Gene = section of DNA → codes for a protein → determines a characteristic. Genome = all genes in an organism.

subject: Biology
question_text: How many chromosomes does a normal human body cell contain?
explanation: Human body cells contain 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs (one from each parent).
correction_tip: 46 chromosomes in body cells (23 pairs). Sex cells (gametes) have 23 (haploid). After fertilisation: 46 restored.

subject: Biology
question_text: What are alleles?
option_a: Different versions of the same gene
option_b: Sections of RNA in the cytoplasm
option_c: Chromosomes that come from the same parent
option_d: Proteins produced by genes
