option_d: It increased global temperatures, melting ice and forming oceans
explanation: As oxygen levels rose via photosynthesis, O₂ in the upper atmosphere was converted to O₃ (ozone) by UV radiation. The ozone layer then absorbed UV, protecting the surface and enabling life to colonise land ~500 million years ago.
correction_tip: Ozone layer formation: O₂ → O₃ in stratosphere (UV driven). This UV shield allowed life to leave oceans and colonise land. Ozone appeared ~500 million years ago.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why do catalytic converters need platinum and rhodium to be effective?
option_a: These metals are cheap and abundant
option_b: Pt and Rh catalyse the reduction of NOₓ to N₂ and oxidation of CO/hydrocarbons; their d-orbitals enable reactant adsorption
option_c: These metals absorb particulate matter
option_d: They increase the temperature of exhaust gases to burn pollutants
explanation: Platinum catalyses oxidation (CO + hydrocarbons → CO₂ + H₂O). Rhodium catalyses reduction (NOₓ → N₂). Both act via d-orbital adsorption. They work only when hot (>200°C), so cold starts pollute more.
correction_tip: Catalytic converter metals: Pt (oxidation catalyst: CO, hydrocarbons), Rh (reduction catalyst: NOₓ → N₂), Pd. All transition metals with d-orbitals for adsorption. Very expensive due to rare metal cost.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A student claims: "CO₂ levels are always rising; they have never been higher than today." Evaluate this using ice core data.
option_a: Correct — CO₂ has never been higher in Earth's history
option_b: Ice cores show CO₂ naturally cycled between ~180 ppm (ice ages) and ~280 ppm (warm periods) over 800,000 years; today's level (~420 ppm) is significantly above any natural level in this record
option_c: Ice cores show CO₂ was higher in the past — so current levels are normal
option_d: CO₂ levels cannot be measured from ice cores
explanation: Ice core data shows CO₂ fluctuated between 180-280 ppm naturally over 800,000 years. Current levels (~420 ppm) are ~50% higher than any natural maximum in that record, indicating human causation.
correction_tip: Ice core CO₂: natural range 180-280 ppm over 800,000 years. Current: ~420 ppm (2024) — far above natural range. Rate of increase also unprecedented. This strongly suggests human cause.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is there debate among scientists about the precise rate of future global warming, even though most agree warming is occurring?
option_a: Scientists disagree on whether warming is happening at all
option_b: Uncertainties in climate sensitivity, feedback strengths, aerosol effects, and future human emissions make precise rate predictions uncertain, even though the direction (warming) is clear
option_c: There is no scientific debate — the exact rate is known precisely
option_d: The debate is purely political, not scientific
explanation: Climate sensitivity (warming per doubling of CO₂), feedback strengths (cloud feedbacks especially), aerosol effects, and future emission trajectories all have uncertainties that affect rate predictions.
correction_tip: Scientific debate: direction of change (warming) = consensus. Rate and magnitude = uncertain due to feedbacks (clouds especially), aerosols, future emissions. 1.5-4.5°C per CO₂ doubling is the IPCC range.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain why reducing NOₓ emissions from cars is challenging despite catalytic converters.
option_a: Catalytic converters cannot reduce NOₓ
option_b: Catalytic converters only work when hot; cold engine starts produce NOₓ before converters reach operating temperature; also, lean-burn diesel engines produce more NOₓ that standard 3-way converters handle poorly
option_c: NOₓ is produced by the catalytic converter itself
option_d: NOₓ reduction requires no converter — engine design changes are sufficient
explanation: 3-way catalytic converters are effective once hot. Cold starts (catalyst <200°C) and lean-burn diesel engines produce NOₓ that standard converters cannot efficiently reduce, requiring SCR (selective catalytic reduction) systems.
correction_tip: NOₓ challenge: 3-way cat needs to be hot; cold starts pollute; diesel engines use lean burn (excess air) → more NOₓ but standard cat less effective in lean conditions → SCR (AdBlue) needed.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: How do scientists use computer models to predict climate change, and what are their limitations?
option_a: Models give exact predictions of future climate
option_b: Climate models use physical equations representing atmosphere/ocean/land interactions; they can project trends but have uncertainties in feedbacks, spatial resolution, and cannot perfectly represent all processes
option_c: Models are unreliable because computers cannot understand chemistry
option_d: Models only predict temperatures; they cannot project sea level or precipitation
explanation: Climate models (GCMs) incorporate atmospheric, oceanic, ice, and land processes. They successfully reproduce past climate changes (validation) but have uncertainties in cloud feedbacks, small-scale processes, and future human behaviour.
correction_tip: Climate models: based on physics/chemistry/biology equations. Validated against past data. Uncertainties: clouds, aerosols, ocean circulation, future emissions. Multiple models give ranges, not single predictions.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain how burning fossil fuels differs from burning biofuels in terms of the carbon cycle.
option_a: Both are identical in their effect on atmospheric CO₂
option_b: Burning fossil fuels releases ancient (millions of years old) carbon previously locked up, permanently increasing atmospheric CO₂. Burning biofuels releases recently-fixed carbon that was recently absorbed from the atmosphere
option_c: Biofuels release more CO₂ than fossil fuels per gram burned
option_d: Fossil fuels and biofuels differ only in their sulfur content
explanation: Fossil fuels add carbon that was removed from the carbon cycle millions of years ago, increasing atmospheric CO₂ permanently (net addition). Biofuels cycle carbon that was recently removed by photosynthesis (approximately carbon neutral).
correction_tip: Fossil fuels: release stored ancient carbon → NET addition to atmosphere. Biofuels: release recently-absorbed carbon → roughly carbon neutral (absorbed by growing crop). Key difference: fossil = new carbon in cycle.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is ground-level ozone (in smog) harmful, while stratospheric ozone is beneficial?
option_a: Both are harmful; stratospheric ozone just causes fewer problems
option_b: Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful UV, protecting organisms. Ground-level ozone (formed in smog) is a powerful oxidant that damages lung tissue, irritates eyes, and damages crops
option_c: Ozone at any level is beneficial; the problem with smog is other pollutants
option_d: Ground-level ozone cools the atmosphere while stratospheric ozone warms it
explanation: Stratospheric ozone (15-35 km) blocks UV radiation — essential protection. Tropospheric/ground-level ozone forms in photochemical smog and is a lung irritant and oxidising pollutant.
correction_tip: Ozone: good high up (blocks UV), bad low down (lung irritant, crop damage). Ground-level O₃ formed from NOₓ + hydrocarbons + sunlight in smog. Stratospheric O₃ = ozone layer.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Discuss whether individual actions or government policy is more effective at reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
option_a: Individual actions are always more effective
option_b: Both are needed: government policy (carbon taxes, emissions regulations, renewable investment) creates systemic change at scale; individual actions (diet, travel, energy use) are meaningful but insufficient alone
option_c: Government policy is entirely ineffective; only individuals can change
option_d: Neither is effective — technology alone will solve climate change
explanation: Systemic change (energy infrastructure, building standards, transport policy) requires government action at scale. Individual actions matter but cannot alone address the structural causes of emissions.
correction_tip: Climate action: individual (reduce flights, plant-based diet, energy efficiency) + government (carbon pricing, renewable energy policy, EV mandates) + international agreements. All three scales needed.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: The Keeling Curve shows CO₂ rising from 315 ppm in 1958 to ~420 ppm in 2024. Calculate the percentage increase and explain the seasonal oscillations visible in the data.
option_a: 25% increase; oscillations caused by tides
option_b: 33% increase; seasonal oscillations caused by Northern Hemisphere plants photosynthesising more in summer (dipping CO₂) and releasing CO₂ in winter decomposition
option_c: 50% increase; oscillations caused by volcanic eruptions
option_d: 5% increase; oscillations are measurement errors
explanation: (420-315)/315 × 100 = 33% increase. Seasonal oscillations: summer → more photosynthesis (NH has more land) → CO₂ dips; winter → less photosynthesis, more decomposition → CO₂ rises. Amplitude ~6 ppm.
correction_tip: Keeling Curve: (420-315)/315 = 33% rise. Seasonal wobble: NH summer = more photosynthesis → CO₂ dip (~3 ppm). NH winter = less photosynthesis → CO₂ rise. Northern hemisphere dominates due to more land area.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Evaluate the evidence that NOₓ emissions from vehicles cause measurable harm to human health in cities.
option_a: There is no reliable evidence linking NOₓ to health outcomes
option_b: Epidemiological studies show correlations between NO₂ exposure and increased asthma, respiratory disease, cardiovascular disease, and premature mortality; natural experiments (lockdowns in 2020) showed measurable health improvements when traffic reduced
option_c: NOₓ only affects people with pre-existing conditions, so general population is safe
option_d: Only SO₂, not NOₓ, has demonstrated health effects
explanation: Extensive epidemiological evidence links urban NO₂ exposure to respiratory and cardiovascular disease. WHO air quality guidelines reflect this. COVID-19 lockdowns provided natural experiments confirming the link.
correction_tip: NOₓ health evidence: epidemiology (population studies), WHO guidelines (NO₂ < 10 μg/m³), lockdown studies (air quality improved → fewer respiratory admissions), mechanistic (inflammation, airway damage).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain how negative feedback from chemical weathering of silicate rocks helps regulate Earth's CO₂ over geological timescales.
option_a: Weathering has no effect on atmospheric CO₂
option_b: Higher temperatures increase weathering of silicate rocks, consuming CO₂ (CaSiO₃ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + SiO₂). This removes CO₂, cooling climate — a negative feedback over millions of years (Urey reaction)
option_c: Weathering increases atmospheric CO₂
option_d: Weathering affects only nitrogen, not carbon
explanation: The Urey reaction: CaSiO₃ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + SiO₂ removes CO₂ from atmosphere. Higher T → more weathering → more CO₂ removed → cooling. Over millions of years, this stabilises climate.
correction_tip: Silicate weathering feedback: warm → faster weathering → more CO₂ consumed → cooling. Negative feedback. Operates over millions of years. Why Earth has not had runaway greenhouse like Venus.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Analyse why the Montreal Protocol (banning CFCs) has been more successful than the Kyoto Protocol (reducing CO₂ emissions).
option_a: Montreal and Kyoto have been equally successful
option_b: Montreal: universal ratification, clear technical alternatives (HFCs), measurable ozone recovery. Kyoto: complex economic trade-offs, developing nations exempt, USA withdrew, limited emissions reduction achieved
option_c: Kyoto was more successful because more countries signed it
option_d: Montreal failed; CFCs are still increasing
explanation: The Montreal Protocol worked because: CFCs had clear substitutes, problem was unambiguous, all nations agreed. Kyoto failed because CO₂ reduction requires economic sacrifice, developed vs developing nation tensions, and no enforcement.
correction_tip: Montreal success: simple substitutes (HFCs), universal buy-in, clear measurable target (ozone hole). Kyoto struggles: economic costs, equity issues, no enforcement mechanism. Paris Agreement (2015) more inclusive.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why might switching from petrol to electric vehicles (EVs) not eliminate all air pollution in cities?
option_a: EVs produce more exhaust gases than petrol cars
option_b: EVs produce no exhaust emissions but still produce tyre and brake wear particles (non-exhaust particulate matter); electricity generation may still use fossil fuels producing emissions elsewhere
option_c: EVs are not significantly cleaner than petrol cars
option_d: EVs produce CO₂ directly from the battery
explanation: EVs eliminate exhaust PM and NOₓ. However: (1) tyre/brake wear releases non-exhaust particles; (2) battery charging from fossil fuels shifts emissions to power plants; (3) manufacturing EVs produces emissions.
correction_tip: EVs reduce tailpipe emissions but: tyre/brake wear particles remain, electricity source matters (coal power = displaced emissions), manufacturing impact. Better than petrol overall, but not zero-impact.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Scientists use carbon isotope ratios (¹³C/¹²C) to attribute climate change to human activities. Explain the logic of this attribution.
option_a: ¹³C/¹²C ratios in the atmosphere are irrelevant to climate attribution
option_b: Fossil fuels have low ¹³C/¹²C because ancient organisms preferentially incorporated ¹²C. Burning fossil fuels adds ¹²C-rich CO₂ → atmospheric ¹³C/¹²C decreases → "isotopic signature" proves fossil fuel origin
option_c: Fossil fuels have high ¹³C and add ¹³C to the atmosphere
option_d: All CO₂ has identical isotope ratios regardless of source
explanation: Photosynthesis preferentially fixes ¹²CO₂, making organic matter depleted in ¹³C. Fossil fuels, derived from ancient organisms, are ¹³C-depleted. Atmospheric ¹³C/¹²C has declined since industrialisation — a fingerprint of fossil fuel burning.
correction_tip: Carbon isotope fingerprinting: plants prefer ¹²C → fossil fuels are ¹³C-depleted. Burning them → atmospheric ¹³C/¹²C falls. Measured decline since 1850 confirms fossil fuel source of rising CO₂.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Describe the role of the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) and explain why it represents scientific consensus rather than advocacy.
option_a: The IPCC is a political body that manufactures climate data
option_b: The IPCC reviews and synthesises thousands of peer-reviewed scientific studies, producing assessments representing the consensus of thousands of scientists worldwide. It assesses evidence and quantifies uncertainty without political advocacy
option_c: The IPCC conducts its own original climate research
option_d: The IPCC only represents the views of wealthy nations' scientists
explanation: The IPCC synthesises existing peer-reviewed science from thousands of researchers worldwide. It quantifies confidence levels and uncertainties transparently, representing scientific consensus rather than advocacy.
correction_tip: IPCC: synthesises peer-reviewed science (does not conduct original research), represents 195 countries, quantifies uncertainty (likelihood statements), multiple Working Groups (science, impacts, mitigation).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is a finite (non-renewable) resource?
option_a: A resource that can be grown and replaced quickly
option_b: A resource that will eventually run out because it cannot be replaced at the rate it is being used
option_c: A resource that exists in unlimited quantities
option_d: A resource that produces no waste
explanation: Finite resources (e.g. fossil fuels, metal ores) take millions of years to form and are being used much faster than they can be replaced. They will eventually be exhausted.
correction_tip: Finite = non-renewable = will run out. E.g. fossil fuels, metal ores. Renewable = can be replaced (e.g. timber, solar energy).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is an ore?
option_a: A pure metal
option_b: A rock containing a sufficient concentration of a metal compound to make extraction worthwhile
option_c: A type of alloy
option_d: A metal that requires no processing
explanation: An ore is a rock that contains enough of a metal compound to make it economically worthwhile to extract the metal from it.
correction_tip: Ore = rock with enough metal compound to extract economically. E.g. haematite (Fe₂O₃) is iron ore; malachite (Cu₂CO₃(OH)₂) is copper ore.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: How is iron extracted from its ore in a blast furnace?
option_a: By electrolysis
option_b: By reduction with carbon (coke)
option_c: By heating with water
option_d: By reaction with acid
explanation: In a blast furnace, iron oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide (produced from coke): Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. The iron melts and runs to the bottom.
correction_tip: Blast furnace: iron ore + coke + limestone + hot air → iron + slag. Iron reduced by CO. Metals above carbon in reactivity series need electrolysis; below can use carbon reduction.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon?
option_a: Aluminium does not occur as an ore
option_b: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce it
option_c: Electrolysis is cheaper than using carbon
option_d: Carbon would contaminate the aluminium
explanation: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so it cannot be reduced by carbon. Electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) is used instead.
correction_tip: Reactivity series: metals more reactive than carbon → electrolysis (Al, Mg, Na). Metals less reactive than carbon → carbon reduction (Fe, Cu). Carbon can only reduce less reactive metals.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the main purpose of the Haber process?
option_a: To produce sulfuric acid
option_b: To produce ammonia for fertilisers
option_c: To extract iron from ore
option_d: To purify copper by electrolysis
explanation: The Haber process combines nitrogen from air with hydrogen to make ammonia (NH₃), which is mainly used to produce fertilisers to increase food production.
correction_tip: Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Conditions: 450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst. Main use: fertiliser production. Feeds roughly half the world's population.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the main use of sulfuric acid produced in the Contact process?
option_a: Food preservation
option_b: Fertiliser and industrial chemical production
option_c: Fuel for cars
option_d: Water purification
explanation: Sulfuric acid is one of the most important industrial chemicals. It is used in fertiliser production, cleaning metals (pickling), batteries, and manufacturing many chemicals.
correction_tip: H₂SO₄ uses: fertilisers (superphosphate), car batteries, making detergents, cleaning metals. Contact process: SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃, then SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What process is used to make seawater drinkable?
option_a: Filtration only
option_b: Distillation or reverse osmosis (desalination)
option_c: Adding chlorine only
option_d: Boiling in sunlight
explanation: Seawater is desalinated by distillation (heating until water evaporates, then condensing) or reverse osmosis (forcing water through a semi-permeable membrane under pressure).
correction_tip: Desalination: distillation or reverse osmosis. Both remove dissolved salts. Very energy-intensive. Used in water-scarce regions (Middle East, parts of Australia).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is recycling and why is it important for metals?
option_a: Melting down used metals and reforming them for new uses
option_b: Burying used metals underground
option_c: Chemically breaking metals down into atoms
option_d: Only applies to paper and plastic
explanation: Recycling metals involves melting down scrap metal and reforming it. This conserves finite metal ores, reduces energy use (much less energy than extracting from ore), and reduces waste.
correction_tip: Metal recycling: conserves ore resources, uses less energy (e.g. recycling aluminium uses ~5% energy vs extraction), reduces waste and pollution. Steel, aluminium, copper all widely recycled.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What does LCA (Life Cycle Assessment) evaluate?
option_a: How long a product lasts before breaking
option_b: The environmental impact of a product throughout its entire life from raw material extraction to disposal
option_c: The cost of producing a product
option_d: The chemical reactions involved in making a product
explanation: An LCA evaluates the total environmental impact at every stage: extraction of raw materials, manufacturing, transportation, use, and disposal/recycling.
correction_tip: LCA: all stages = cradle-to-grave. Stages: raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, disposal. Helps compare environmental impact of different products.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is phytomining?
option_a: Mining with robots
option_b: Growing plants that absorb metal ions from low-grade ore soil, then burning them to produce ash rich in metal compounds
option_c: Extracting metals using plant-derived acids
option_d: A type of electroplating
explanation: Phytomining uses plants that hyperaccumulate metals (e.g. copper). The plants are harvested and burned; the ash contains a much higher concentration of metal compounds that can be extracted.
correction_tip: Phytomining: hyperaccumulator plants absorb metal → harvest plants → burn → metal-rich ash → extract metal. Used for copper from low-grade ores. Less environmentally damaging than traditional mining.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the purpose of adding chlorine to drinking water?
option_a: To improve taste
option_b: To kill microorganisms and make it safe to drink
option_c: To remove calcium ions
option_d: To increase the pH
explanation: Chlorine is added to drinking water as a disinfectant to kill bacteria, viruses, and other microorganisms that could cause disease.
correction_tip: Water treatment: filter (remove particles) → add chlorine (kill microbes) → add fluoride (optional, tooth decay prevention). Chlorination is essential for public health.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is bioleaching?
option_a: Growing plants over mine sites
option_b: Using bacteria to extract metal ions from low-grade ores by producing acidic conditions
option_c: Heating ores with concentrated acid
option_d: Using electric current to extract metals
explanation: Bioleaching uses bacteria (e.g. Acidithiobacillus) that oxidise sulfide minerals, releasing metal ions (e.g. copper) into solution. The metal-rich solution is then processed to extract the metal.
correction_tip: Bioleaching: bacteria oxidise sulfide ores → release Cu²⁺ ions → scrap iron displaces copper (displacement reaction) OR electrolysis. Used for low-grade copper ores.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What are the three Rs of sustainable resource use?
option_a: Remove, Replace, Renew
option_b: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
option_c: Refine, Reform, Recover
option_d: Research, React, Remove
explanation: The 3Rs: Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again), Recycle (process and use material again). All help conserve finite resources and reduce environmental impact.
correction_tip: 3Rs: Reduce (best — use less), Reuse (use same item again), Recycle (process into new material). In order of environmental preference: reduce first.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the main raw material used to make glass?
option_a: Limestone
option_b: Sand (silicon dioxide, SiO₂)
option_c: Salt
option_d: Clay
explanation: Glass is mainly made from sand (SiO₂, silicon dioxide) mixed with soda ash (Na₂CO₃) and limestone (CaCO₃), then heated to high temperatures.
correction_tip: Glass: sand (SiO₂) + soda ash (Na₂CO₃) + limestone (CaCO₃) → heated → glass. Raw materials are abundant. Glass is 100% recyclable.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the main advantage of using composites over traditional materials?
option_a: They are always cheaper to produce
option_b: They combine properties of two or more materials, giving better performance than either alone
option_c: They are all biodegradable
option_d: They replace the need for all metals
explanation: Composites (e.g. carbon fibre reinforced polymer) combine the properties of different materials — for example, high strength from carbon fibre and low weight from the polymer matrix.
correction_tip: Composites: combine properties of component materials. E.g. carbon fibre reinforced plastic (CFRP): strong like carbon fibre + light like polymer. Used in aircraft, sports equipment.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is recycling aluminium much more energy-efficient than extracting it from bauxite?
option_a: Aluminium does not need to be melted for recycling
option_b: Extraction from bauxite requires electrolysis at very high temperatures (energy intensive); recycling only requires melting the aluminium (~5% of the extraction energy)
option_c: Bauxite contains impurities that need to be removed first
option_d: Recycled aluminium is always purer than extracted aluminium
explanation: Electrolytic extraction of aluminium from molten Al₂O₃ requires enormous amounts of electricity. Recycling only needs to melt the metal, using approximately 5% of the energy.
correction_tip: Al extraction: electrolysis of molten Al₂O₃ at ~960°C → very high energy. Recycling: melt Al (~660°C melting point) → ~5% energy. Huge energy saving → strong economic and environmental argument for recycling Al.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Describe the stages of treating river water to make it safe to drink.
option_a: Only add chlorine
option_b: Sedimentation (large particles settle), filtration (through sand/gravel removes smaller particles), chlorination (kills microorganisms), pH adjustment
option_c: Only filter and add fluoride
option_d: Boil, then add salt
explanation: Water treatment: (1) screening/sedimentation — large particles removed; (2) coagulation (alum added) — fine particles clump; (3) filtration — through sand/gravel; (4) chlorination — disinfection.
correction_tip: Water treatment stages: sedimentation/settling → coagulation (alum) → filtration (sand) → chlorination (disinfection) → pH adjustment (if needed). Each stage removes different contaminants.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: How is copper extracted from a copper sulfate solution using scrap iron (displacement)?
option_a: Iron dissolves in the solution and copper precipitates: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu
option_b: Copper dissolves to form copper sulfate and iron precipitates
option_c: The iron reacts with sulfate ions only
option_d: No reaction occurs between iron and copper sulfate
explanation: Iron is more reactive than copper, so iron displaces copper from copper sulfate solution. Iron atoms give electrons to Cu²⁺ ions, which deposit as copper metal.
correction_tip: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. Iron (more reactive) displaces copper (less reactive). Iron dissolved; copper deposited. Used in bioleaching after bacteria dissolve copper from ore.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the advantage of phytomining over traditional copper mining for low-grade ores?
option_a: Phytomining extracts copper faster
option_b: Phytomining causes less environmental damage, requires no heavy machinery, and can be used on land where traditional mining is not economical
option_c: Phytomining produces purer copper
option_d: Phytomining requires no energy
explanation: Phytomining is useful for low-grade ores where traditional mining is uneconomic. It causes much less surface disruption, generates less waste rock, and can even be used for land remediation.
correction_tip: Phytomining advantages: low environmental impact, works on low-grade ores, no heavy machinery needed, can remediate contaminated land. Disadvantage: slow (multiple growing seasons), limited scale.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What are the limitations of LCA (Life Cycle Assessment)?
option_a: LCA gives completely objective results with no uncertainty
option_b: Subjective judgements are made about the importance of different stages; data may be incomplete; different assessors can reach different conclusions for the same product
option_c: LCA only considers manufacturing, not disposal
option_d: LCA cannot be applied to metal products
explanation: LCA involves subjective decisions about which impacts to prioritise (e.g. energy vs water vs land use). Data quality varies, and different assumptions can lead to different conclusions. LCA can be used selectively to support a predetermined view.
correction_tip: LCA limitations: subjective (which impacts to weight more?), data incomplete, can be used to "greenwash" (selecting favourable comparisons), results depend on assumptions. Not purely objective.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the difference between pure metals and alloys in terms of properties?
option_a: Pure metals are always harder than alloys
option_b: Pure metals have regular structures that slip easily (soft, malleable); alloys have different-sized atoms disrupting the layers, making them harder and less malleable
option_c: Alloys have fewer electrons and are less conductive
option_d: There is no difference — pure metals and alloys have identical properties
explanation: Pure metals have uniform atomic structures where layers slide over each other easily. Alloys contain different-sized atoms that distort the structure, preventing layer movement → harder, stronger.
correction_tip: Pure metal: regular layers → slide easily → soft. Alloy: mixed atom sizes → distorted layers → harder. E.g. pure iron is soft; steel (Fe+C) is much harder.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is water described as a "universal solvent" and why is this a problem for water treatment?
option_a: Water dissolves all substances, making purification impossible
option_b: Water dissolves many substances (ionic compounds, polar molecules); natural water contains dissolved minerals, pollutants and microorganisms that must be removed for safe drinking
option_c: Water is a solvent only for organic molecules
option_d: Water's dissolving ability means it cannot be treated chemically
explanation: Water's polar nature means it dissolves many ionic and polar substances. Natural water sources contain dissolved salts, pesticides, heavy metals, and microorganisms — all requiring treatment.
correction_tip: Water as solvent: good at dissolving ionic/polar substances. Natural water contains: dissolved minerals (hard water), pollutants (pesticides, heavy metals), microorganisms. All need removal.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the difference between thermosetting and thermosoftening polymers in terms of recycling?
option_a: Both types can be recycled equally easily
option_b: Thermosoftening polymers can be melted and remoulded (recyclable); thermosetting polymers have permanent cross-links and cannot be melted (not recyclable by conventional methods)
option_c: Only thermosetting polymers can be recycled
option_d: Neither type can be recycled
explanation: Thermosoftening polymers have weak intermolecular forces and soften on heating — they can be recycled. Thermosetting polymers have strong covalent cross-links that cannot be broken by heating.
correction_tip: Thermosoftening: weak IMFs between chains → melts on heating → recyclable. E.g. poly(ethene). Thermosetting: covalent cross-links → doesn't melt → not recyclable by melting. E.g. Bakelite.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is it important to conserve metal ores?
option_a: Metal ores are renewable and will replace themselves quickly
option_b: Metal ores are finite resources that take millions of years to form; conserving them means future generations will have access to these materials
option_c: Conservation reduces the quality of metals extracted
option_d: Conservation is only important for precious metals like gold
explanation: Metal ores form over geological timescales (millions of years) and are non-renewable. Once extracted, they cannot be replaced. Conservation through recycling and efficient use ensures future availability.
correction_tip: Metal ores are finite and non-renewable. At current rates, some ores (copper, rare earth metals) could be depleted within decades. Recycling, phytomining, bioleaching = alternatives to new extraction.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain how the NPK ratio on a fertiliser bag indicates its composition.
option_a: NPK stands for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium proportions by mass
option_b: NPK stands for nitrogen, potassium, and calcium
option_c: NPK only indicates total nitrogen content
option_d: NPK refers to the manufacturing process
explanation: NPK ratios give the percentages of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P₂O₅ equivalent), and potassium (K₂O equivalent) in a fertiliser. Different crops and soils need different ratios.
correction_tip: NPK: N=nitrogen (leaf growth), P=phosphorus (root/fruit), K=potassium (flower/fruit, disease resistance). A 10:5:5 fertiliser has 10% N, 5% P, 5% K.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is hard water and how does it form?
option_a: Water with a high temperature
option_b: Water containing dissolved Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions from rainwater dissolving limestone and dolomite rocks
option_c: Water with a low pH
option_d: Water from glaciers and ice caps
explanation: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions picked up when water flows through limestone (CaCO₃) and dolomite (CaMg(CO₃)₂) rocks. It forms scum with soap and limescale in pipes.
correction_tip: Hard water: Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions dissolved from limestone. Problems: scum with soap, limescale in pipes/boilers (wasted energy). Softened by ion exchange or adding sodium carbonate.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What environmental problems are caused by mining for metals?
option_a: Mining has no environmental impact
option_b: Habitat destruction, noise and dust pollution, acid mine drainage, toxic waste tailings, and landscape scarring
option_c: Mining only affects air quality, not land or water
option_d: Only underground mining causes environmental damage
explanation: Mining causes: destruction of habitats and ecosystems, dust and noise pollution, acid mine drainage (sulfide minerals + water → H₂SO₄), toxic tailings leaching into groundwater, landscape disruption.
correction_tip: Mining impacts: habitat loss, acid drainage (sulfide oxidation → H₂SO₄ → toxic to aquatic life), heavy metal leaching, dust, noise. Remediation is expensive. Why recycling and phytomining are preferred.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is steel more useful than pure iron for construction?
option_a: Steel is cheaper than iron
option_b: Steel (iron + carbon) is stronger and harder than pure iron, and can be made with specific properties by varying carbon content and adding other metals
option_c: Steel has lower density than pure iron
option_d: Steel does not corrode at all
explanation: Pure iron is soft due to its regular atomic structure. Adding carbon (and other metals like nickel, chromium) produces steel alloys with much greater strength, hardness, and specific properties for different uses.
correction_tip: Steel: iron + carbon (0.1-2%). Higher carbon = harder but more brittle. Stainless steel: Fe + Cr + Ni = corrosion resistant. Different steels for different purposes (springs, cutlery, structural).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the Contact process and what is its main product?
option_a: A process for extracting iron from ore
option_b: An industrial process making sulfuric acid: SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃ (with V₂O₅ catalyst), then SO₃ absorbed in H₂SO₄ to make oleum, then diluted with water
option_c: A process for producing ammonia
option_d: A process for polymerisation of ethene
explanation: The Contact process makes sulfuric acid. Key step: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ using V₂O₅ catalyst at 450°C. SO₃ is absorbed in H₂SO₄ to form oleum (H₂S₂O₇), then diluted to give H₂SO₄.
correction_tip: Contact process: makes H₂SO₄. SO₂+½O₂→SO₃ (V₂O₅, 450°C). SO₃+H₂O→H₂SO₄ (but direct addition too vigorous → use oleum first). Conditions: 450°C (compromise, V₂O₅ helps), 1-2 atm.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Copper can be extracted from low-grade ores by bioleaching using Acidithiobacillus bacteria. Explain the mechanism and how copper is recovered.
option_a: Bacteria directly melt the ore to release copper
option_b: Bacteria oxidise copper sulfide minerals, releasing Cu²⁺ ions into acidic solution; copper is then recovered by displacement with scrap iron (Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu) or by electrolysis
option_c: Bacteria absorb copper internally and are harvested for their copper content
option_d: Bacteria produce acid that reacts with carbonate gangue only
explanation: Acidithiobacillus bacteria oxidise CuFeS₂ (chalcopyrite), releasing Cu²⁺ into the leachate. Scrap iron displaces copper (displacement reaction) or electrolysis purifies it. Very slow but low environmental impact.
correction_tip: Bioleaching: bacteria oxidise Cu sulfide → Cu²⁺ in solution → add scrap iron: Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu (displacement). Or electrolyse leachate. Slow (months/years) but works on <0.5% grade ore.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Compare the environmental impact of reverse osmosis desalination versus traditional river water treatment.
option_a: Both have identical environmental impacts
option_b: Reverse osmosis uses significantly more energy per litre than river treatment; it also produces a concentrated brine waste stream; river treatment is more efficient but requires a freshwater source
option_c: River treatment uses more energy than reverse osmosis
option_d: Reverse osmosis produces no waste at all
explanation: Reverse osmosis requires high-pressure pumps (~50-80 bar) → high energy use. It also produces concentrated brine that must be disposed of carefully (harm to marine ecosystems if discharged inappropriately). River treatment requires much less energy.
correction_tip: Reverse osmosis: high energy (high pressure needed), brine waste, used where no freshwater available. River treatment: lower energy, uses existing freshwater infrastructure. Energy source matters for RO carbon footprint.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Evaluate the use of LCA to compare a paper bag with a plastic bag in terms of environmental impact.
option_a: Paper bags are always more environmentally friendly
option_b: LCA shows paper bags use more energy and water in production and are heavier (more transport emissions), while plastic bags use less energy to produce but persist as pollution. Result depends on assumptions and number of reuses
option_c: Plastic bags are always worse — they take longer to degrade
option_d: Both bags have identical LCAs
explanation: Paper bag LCA: more energy/water in production, biodegradable, heavier. Plastic bag LCA: less energy to produce, very long-lasting (pollution risk), lighter. A plastic bag reused many times can outperform paper on energy grounds.
correction_tip: LCA: paper bags — more energy/water to make, heavier (transport), biodegradable. Plastic bags — less energy to make, lighter, durable but persistent pollution. Context matters — number of uses is key.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain why the production of steel from scrap (electric arc furnace) produces less CO₂ than from iron ore in a blast furnace.
option_a: The electric arc furnace uses no electricity
option_b: Blast furnace needs coke (carbon from coal) as reductant, producing large amounts of CO₂. Electric arc furnace melts scrap steel using electricity, with no carbon reduction step required
option_c: Both processes produce identical CO₂ emissions
option_d: Blast furnace uses renewable energy; electric arc uses fossil fuels
explanation: Blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ — carbon is chemically consumed as a reductant. EAF: electricity melts existing steel — no carbon needed for chemical reduction.
correction_tip: Blast furnace: coke needed as chemical reductant → CO₂ produced chemically. EAF: only needs energy (electricity) to melt → no chemical CO₂. EAF carbon footprint depends on electricity source.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What are the environmental concerns with using nitrogen fertilisers, and how does this relate to the Haber process?
option_a: Nitrogen fertilisers have no environmental impact
option_b: Excess nitrate from fertilisers leaches into waterways → eutrophication (algal bloom, deoxygenation, fish death). The Haber process itself uses fossil fuels, so ammonia production has a significant carbon footprint
option_c: Fertilisers only affect air quality
option_d: The Haber process produces no greenhouse gases
explanation: Nitrate leaching causes eutrophication. Haber process: requires fossil fuels (natural gas for H₂, energy for high P and T) → significant CO₂ emissions. Research into green ammonia (using renewable energy for H₂) aims to address this.
correction_tip: Fertiliser problems: nitrate leaching → eutrophication (algae → decomposition → O₂ depletion → fish death). Haber process carbon footprint: ~1-2% global CO₂ from natural gas use.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is fluoride sometimes added to drinking water, and what are the arguments against this practice?
option_a: Fluoride improves the taste of water
option_b: Fluoride at low levels (1 ppm) reduces tooth decay. Arguments against: mass medication without individual consent; some studies suggest high fluoride levels harm bones/thyroid; natural fluoride levels vary and some areas exceed safe limits
option_c: Fluoride removes all bacteria from water
option_d: Fluoride prevents water from being too acidic
explanation: Water fluoridation reduces childhood tooth decay (proven benefit). Concerns: dental/skeletal fluorosis at high concentrations; ethical questions about adding medication to water without individual consent; some dispute the data.
correction_tip: Fluoridation: proven to reduce tooth decay. Controversy: forced medication without consent, fluorosis risk at high levels, ecological effects. Many countries fluoridate; others do not. Contested public health policy.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why are rare earth metals increasingly important and why is their extraction problematic?
option_a: Rare earths are abundant and easy to extract
option_b: Rare earth metals are essential for modern technology (electric motors, wind turbines, smartphones). Their extraction causes radioactive waste, toxic chemicals, and vast landscape destruction; most deposits are in politically unstable regions
option_c: Rare earth metals are only used in jewellery
option_d: Rare earth extraction has no environmental problems
explanation: Rare earths (neodymium, dysprosium, etc.) are critical for EV motors, wind turbines, and electronics. Extraction produces radioactive thorium/uranium waste, toxic acids, and landscape damage. ~80% production in China.
correction_tip: Rare earths: essential for green tech (EV motors, wind turbines). Problems: toxic/radioactive waste, supply concentrated in few countries, no good recycling processes. Irony: "green" technology has environmentally costly materials.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain why shape memory alloys (like nitinol) are useful in medicine.
option_a: They are insoluble in body fluids
option_b: They return to a pre-set shape when heated to body temperature, allowing stents to expand in blood vessels and orthodontic wires to maintain constant force
option_c: They dissolve and are absorbed by the body over time
option_d: They conduct electricity better than any other alloy
explanation: Nitinol (Ni-Ti alloy) can be deformed at low temperature and returns to its original shape when warmed. In medicine: cardiac stents that expand when placed in a warm blood vessel; dental braces that apply continuous force.
correction_tip: Shape memory alloys (nitinol): deformed cold → returns to shape when warmed. Uses: cardiac stents (expand in artery at body temperature), orthodontic braces (continuous light force), surgical staples.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the difference between biodegradable and non-biodegradable polymers in terms of environmental impact?
option_a: Biodegradable polymers are always better environmentally
option_b: Biodegradable polymers can be broken down by microorganisms, reducing landfill accumulation. But they may break down too fast, require specific composting conditions, or release CH₄. Non-biodegradable polymers persist (pollution) but can be recycled
option_c: Non-biodegradable polymers are better because they last longer
option_d: Both types are identical in environmental impact
explanation: Biodegradable polymers reduce long-term plastic accumulation but need industrial composting conditions and may produce methane (greenhouse gas) in landfill. Non-biodegradable plastics are persistent but can potentially be mechanically or chemically recycled.
correction_tip: Biodegradable: breaks down → less long-term pollution. But needs right conditions; may release CH₄ in landfill (worse than CO₂ per molecule). Non-biodegradable: persistent → pollution. Can be recycled but collection rates low.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain how ion exchange resins soften hard water and what the advantages and disadvantages are.
option_a: Ion exchange resins add sodium carbonate to precipitate calcium
option_b: Resin contains Na⁺ ions; Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ swap with Na⁺, removing hardness. Advantages: effective, continuous. Disadvantages: requires regeneration with salt, adds Na⁺ (health concern for some)
option_c: Ion exchange removes chlorine from water
option_d: The resin filters particles but not ions
explanation: Ion exchange resins exchange Na⁺ (or H⁺) for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, removing hardness. The resin is regenerated with concentrated NaCl solution (brine). Disadvantage: increased sodium in water, salt use.
correction_tip: Ion exchange: resin-Na⁺ + Ca²⁺ → resin-Ca²⁺ + Na⁺. Removes hardness by removing Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺. Disadvantages: needs regenerating with salt, adds sodium to water (concern for hypertension patients).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is electrolytic refining of copper and why is it necessary?
option_a: It produces copper from copper ore
option_b: It purifies impure copper: impure Cu anode dissolves; pure Cu deposits on cathode; impurities (gold, silver) fall as anode sludge
option_c: It converts copper to copper sulfate for storage
option_d: It coats steel with copper for corrosion protection
explanation: Electrolytic refining: impure Cu anode, pure Cu cathode, CuSO₄ electrolyte. Cu²⁺ ions from anode deposit at cathode. Precious metal impurities (Au, Ag) fall as anode sludge — valuable by-product.
correction_tip: Copper refining: anode (impure Cu) → Cu²⁺ ions → deposit on cathode (pure Cu). Impurities fall as anode sludge. Required because electrical grade copper must be >99.99% pure for conductivity.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Evaluate the sustainability of using natural gas as a source of hydrogen for the Haber process.
option_a: Natural gas is the most sustainable hydrogen source
option_b: Natural gas (CH₄ + H₂O → CO + H₂, steam reforming) uses fossil fuels, producing CO₂. Not sustainable long-term. Green hydrogen (electrolysis of water using renewable energy) is more sustainable but currently more expensive
option_c: Hydrogen from natural gas produces no greenhouse gases
option_d: The Haber process does not require hydrogen
explanation: Current Haber process uses H₂ from steam reforming of natural gas (grey hydrogen), producing CO₂. Green ammonia uses H₂ from renewable-powered electrolysis, reducing the carbon footprint to near-zero.
correction_tip: Grey H₂: natural gas + steam → H₂ + CO₂ (greenhouse gas). Green H₂: water electrolysis using renewable electricity → H₂ + O₂ (no CO₂). Green ammonia = Haber process with green H₂. Currently 3-5× more expensive.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: How does the production of nanoparticles raise new challenges for LCA?
option_a: Nanoparticles are too small to assess in LCA
option_b: Traditional LCA methods do not fully account for the unique risks of nanoparticles (potential toxicity at low doses, persistence, novel pathways); data on nanoparticle lifecycle impacts is still limited
option_c: LCA shows nanoparticles have no environmental impact
option_d: Nanoparticles are identical to bulk materials in LCA terms
explanation: Nanoparticle behaviour (toxicity, persistence, environmental fate) can differ significantly from bulk materials. LCA frameworks are still being developed to properly account for nano-specific impacts.
correction_tip: Nanoparticle LCA challenges: unique toxicity (can cross biological barriers), environmental persistence, behaviour differs from bulk material, limited data on manufacturing impacts, new risk assessment methods needed.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A mining company claims bioleaching is always more environmentally friendly than conventional mining. Evaluate this claim.
option_a: Completely correct — bioleaching has zero environmental impact
option_b: Mostly true (less landscape disruption, lower energy) but: acid mine drainage from bacterial activity can pollute groundwater; slow release of heavy metals; long timeframes mean sustained monitoring needed
option_c: Completely false — bioleaching causes more damage
option_d: Only applies to gold, not copper
explanation: Bioleaching avoids open-cast mining disruption and uses less energy. However, the acidic bacterial conditions can leach toxic metals into groundwater, and the process is very slow (years). Full LCA needed.
correction_tip: Bioleaching pros: less landscape damage, less energy, works on low-grade ore. Cons: acidic drainage can pollute groundwater/streams, slow (years), monitoring needed. Not automatically better than conventional mining.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: The global demand for lithium (for batteries) is projected to increase 10-fold by 2050. Analyse the sustainability challenges this creates.
option_a: Lithium is unlimited — no sustainability issue
option_b: High demand may exhaust known reserves; extraction (hard rock or brine) damages ecosystems and uses large amounts of water in arid regions; recycling infrastructure is underdeveloped; supply chain concentrated in few countries
option_c: Lithium can be synthesised so supply is not an issue
option_d: Only the price, not sustainability, is a concern
explanation: Lithium demand for EV batteries creates: supply concentration risk (Chile, Australia, China); ecological damage from lithium brine extraction (water-scarce Atacama Desert); insufficient recycling; potential shortage affecting EV transition.
correction_tip: Lithium challenges: brine extraction uses massive water in desert (Atacama), ecosystem damage, supply chains vulnerable (few countries), battery recycling not yet at scale. "Green" EVs have critical mineral dependencies.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Evaluate the pros and cons of adding chlorine to drinking water supplies for public health.
option_a: Chlorination is perfect — it has no downsides
option_b: Pros: kills pathogens (prevents cholera, typhoid — saved millions of lives); residual protection in distribution system. Cons: disinfection by-products (trihalomethanes from Cl + organic matter may increase cancer risk); taste/odour issues
option_c: Chlorination is dangerous and should be banned
option_d: Chlorination only kills bacteria, not viruses
explanation: Chlorination has dramatically reduced waterborne disease. But: reaction with natural organic matter produces trihalomethanes (THMs) with possible links to cancer; taste concerns; some resistant pathogens (Cryptosporidium) not killed by Cl.
correction_tip: Chlorination: huge public health benefit (waterborne disease prevention). Concerns: THMs (disinfection by-products, possible carcinogens), taste, Cryptosporidium resistance. Risk-benefit analysis strongly favours chlorination.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Analyse why the circular economy model is considered more sustainable than the traditional linear "take-make-dispose" economy.
option_a: Linear economies are always more efficient
option_b: Circular economy: keeps materials in use through recycling, reuse, and remanufacturing; reduces extraction of finite resources; minimises waste; can be more economically efficient. Linear: finite resources used once → waste; dependent on cheap virgin materials
option_c: Both models have identical sustainability outcomes
option_d: Circular economy is only suitable for metals, not polymers
explanation: Linear economy is unsustainable as it depletes finite resources and creates waste. Circular economy models aim to eliminate waste by keeping materials in use, regenerating natural systems, and decoupling growth from resource use.
correction_tip: Circular economy: reduce → reuse → recycle → recover → eliminate waste. More sustainable: less mining, less waste, lower emissions. Challenges: contamination, collection costs, consumer behaviour change.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: The extraction of titanium requires multiple reduction steps and cannot use carbon reduction. Explain why and describe the Kroll process.
option_a: Titanium can be extracted by carbon reduction at high temperatures
option_b: Titanium is more reactive than carbon and forms stable TiC with carbon. The Kroll process: TiO₂ + 2Cl₂ → TiCl₄, then TiCl₄ + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl₂ (reduction by magnesium, an inert argon atmosphere)
option_c: Titanium is extracted by electrolysis of TiO₂
option_d: Titanium requires no extraction — it exists as native metal
explanation: Carbon reduction of titanium produces TiC (titanium carbide), contaminating the product. The Kroll process uses chlorination followed by reduction with liquid magnesium under argon (inert atmosphere).
correction_tip: Kroll process: TiO₂ → TiCl₄ (chlorination) → Ti (reduction by Mg). Cannot use C (TiC formed). Very energy-intensive and costly → Ti is expensive. Used in aerospace due to Ti's excellent strength-to-weight ratio.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Discuss the ethical issues of selling chemical expertise and technology to developing countries for both fertiliser production and water treatment.
option_a: There are no ethical issues — all technology transfer is beneficial
option_b: Benefits: food security, clean water, poverty reduction. Issues: dependency on imported technology, intellectual property, environmental degradation if poorly regulated, may prioritise export crops over local food security
option_c: Technology should never be transferred between countries
option_d: Ethics only apply to water technology, not fertiliser technology
explanation: Technology transfer can improve living standards. But: IP protection limits access; poorly regulated use can cause environmental damage; trade dependency; fertiliser use can contribute to eutrophication and loss of traditional farming practices.
correction_tip: Technology transfer ethics: benefits (food security, clean water, economic development) vs risks (dependency, IP costs, environmental harm without regulation, economic imperialism). Complex trade-offs.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why might the development of better catalysts for the Haber process be one of the most impactful advances in sustainable chemistry?
option_a: Better catalysts would increase energy consumption
option_b: A catalyst enabling lower temperature and pressure would dramatically reduce energy use (Haber uses ~1% global energy); enabling room-temperature nitrogen fixation (like nitrogenase enzyme in bacteria) would be transformative
option_c: Catalysts cannot improve the Haber process further
option_d: The Haber process already has no environmental impact
explanation: Current Haber conditions (450°C, 200 atm) require enormous energy (~1% world energy). A better catalyst enabling lower T and P (or ambient conditions like biological nitrogenase) would reduce the enormous carbon footprint of fertiliser production.
correction_tip: Haber process uses ~1% of global energy. Nitrogenase enzyme (in bacteria) fixes N₂ at room T and pressure using ATP. Mimicking nitrogenase with a catalyst = potential to revolutionise fertiliser production and save enormous energy.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Evaluate the scientific and ethical issues surrounding whether to add fluoride to drinking water.
option_a: Fluoridation is clearly correct with no counterarguments
option_b: Scientific: fluoride at 1ppm reduces tooth decay (strong evidence); above 4ppm causes dental/skeletal fluorosis. Ethical: benefit vs autonomy (medication without consent), social equity (poor communities benefit most), expert vs public risk perception
option_c: Fluoridation has no ethical dimension
option_d: The science on fluoride is completely uncertain
explanation: Strong evidence supports fluoridation at 1ppm for dental health. The ethical debate centres on: individual autonomy vs population benefit; equity (poorest communities most affected by poor dental health); whether government should medicate water supplies.
correction_tip: Fluoridation debate: science = reduces tooth decay at 1 ppm, fluorosis risk >4 ppm. Ethics = individual freedom vs collective benefit, equity, medication without consent. Policy decision reflects societal values.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What are the key advantages of using corrosion-resistant alloys like stainless steel and anodised aluminium in sustainable construction?
option_a: They are the cheapest materials available
option_b: Longer-lasting materials need less frequent replacement → less mining and manufacturing energy; stainless steel (Cr₂O₃ layer) and anodised Al (Al₂O₃ layer) both resist corrosion through protective oxide layers
option_c: Corrosion resistance is only important in marine environments
option_d: These materials are fully biodegradable
explanation: Corrosion resistance extends material lifetime, reducing replacement frequency and the energy/resources of manufacturing new components. The protective oxide layer (passive film) prevents further corrosion.
correction_tip: Stainless steel: Cr₂O₃ passive layer. Anodised Al: thickened Al₂O₃ layer. Both: longer lifespan → less frequent replacement → less resource use. Sustainable: durability reduces lifetime environmental impact.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Assess the feasibility of recycling rare earth metals from electronic waste ("e-waste") to reduce mining demand.
option_a: E-waste recycling is simple and already supplies all rare earth needs
option_b: E-waste contains valuable rare earths but in tiny amounts, scattered across many complex components. Current recycling rates <1%; challenges include: complex disassembly, many different alloys, lack of collection infrastructure, hazardous materials
option_c: Rare earth metals cannot be recycled under any circumstances
option_d: All rare earths are already recovered from e-waste
explanation: E-waste recycling for rare earths is technically possible but faces major challenges: REE concentrations in devices are very low; devices contain hazardous materials; collection and sorting is costly; REE are mixed with many other materials in complex components.
correction_tip: E-waste rare earth recycling: <1% currently recovered. Barriers: low concentration in devices, complex disassembly, mixed materials, hazardous components, lack of collection systems. Research priority: urban mining, hydrometallurgical recovery.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What does CO2 stand for?
option_a: Carbon oxide
option_b: Carbon dioxide
option_c: Carbon monoxide
option_d: Carbon tetrachloride
explanation: CO2 is carbon dioxide — one carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms. It is the main greenhouse gas produced by burning fossil fuels.
correction_tip: CO2 = carbon dioxide. CO = carbon monoxide. Both produced by combustion; CO2 from complete, CO from incomplete combustion.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is carbon monoxide produced in limited oxygen rather than carbon dioxide?
option_a: Because carbon does not react with oxygen completely
option_b: There is insufficient oxygen to fully oxidise carbon to CO2; carbon is incompletely oxidised, stopping at CO
option_c: Because CO2 requires a catalyst
option_d: Because CO is the more stable molecule
explanation: Complete combustion: C + O2 -> CO2 (excess O2). Incomplete combustion: 2C + O2 -> 2CO (limited O2). Each carbon atom only gets one oxygen atom.
correction_tip: Limited O2: carbon only partially oxidised -> CO (one O per C). Excess O2: full oxidisation -> CO2 (two O per C).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: The percentage of CO2 in today atmosphere is approximately 0.042% (420 ppm). Calculate how many litres of CO2 are in one cubic metre (1000L) of air.
explanation: 0.042% of 1000 L = 0.042/100 x 1000 = 0.42 L of CO2 per cubic metre of air.
correction_tip: 0.042% = 0.00042 fraction. x 1000L = 0.42L CO2 per cubic metre.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Explain why water vapour is considered important in current warming despite CO2 being the primary driver.
option_a: Water vapour is more abundant and acts as the initial forcing that causes warming, while CO2 amplifies it
option_b: CO2 acts as the initial forcing that raises temperature; this increases evaporation, increasing water vapour which amplifies warming as a positive feedback
option_c: CO2 and water vapour have identical effects
option_d: Water vapour decreases with warming, reducing the effect
explanation: CO2 directly raises temperature (forcing). This warming increases evaporation -> more water vapour -> stronger greenhouse effect (feedback). H2O is the most abundant GHG but cannot initiate warming (its level depends on temperature).
correction_tip: CO2 = forcing (causes initial warming). H2O = feedback (amplifies warming). CO2 acts first; H2O responds and amplifies. Both important in different ways.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: A city implements a low-emission zone restricting diesel vehicles. Predict the air quality changes over 3 months.
option_a: NO2 and PM2.5 levels increase as congestion grows
option_b: NO2 and PM2.5 levels decrease as older high-emitting diesel vehicles are excluded, with measurable improvements within weeks based on real-world data
option_c: Air quality is unchanged because only vehicle type, not number, matters
option_d: Only CO2 levels decrease; other pollutants are unaffected
explanation: Low-emission zone exclusion of older higher-emitting diesel vehicles reduces NOx and PM2.5 levels measurably. London ULEZ introduction showed significant NO2 reductions within months.
correction_tip: LEZ/ULEZ evidence: London data shows measurable reduction in NO2 and PM2.5. Older diesel vehicles produce most NOx and particulates per km.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Methane has a global warming potential (GWP) of 80 over 20 years versus CO2. Why does this matter for climate policy?
option_a: It means CH4 causes 80 times less warming than CO2
option_b: Over 20 years, 1 kg of CH4 causes 80x more warming than 1 kg CO2. Reducing methane from livestock, gas leaks, and landfill gives rapid near-term climate benefits
option_c: GWP is irrelevant because CH4 concentrations are lower
option_d: Reducing CO2 is 80x more effective than reducing CH4
explanation: GWP: CH4 absorbs more infrared per molecule and degrades faster (~12 year lifetime vs CO2 centuries). Reducing CH4 gives rapid near-term benefits, important for meeting short-term climate targets.
correction_tip: CH4 GWP=80 (20-yr): very potent but short-lived (~12 yr). Reducing CH4 gives fast climate benefits. For 1.5 degree target, CH4 reduction is crucial for short-term impact.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What raw materials are needed for the Haber process?
option_a: Nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas
option_b: Sulfur dioxide and oxygen
option_c: Iron ore and coke
option_d: Nitrogen from the air and oxygen from electrolysis
explanation: The Haber process uses nitrogen from the air (about 78% N2) and hydrogen mainly from natural gas via steam reforming of CH4.
correction_tip: Haber: N2 (from air) + H2 (from natural gas steam reforming). N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the main environmental benefit of recycling copper?
option_a: Copper becomes cheaper to buy
option_b: Less energy needed and less habitat destruction compared to mining new copper ore
option_c: Recycled copper is purer than mined copper
option_d: Recycling produces more copper than mining
explanation: Recycling copper uses about 85% less energy than extracting it from ore and avoids habitat destruction from open-cast mining.
correction_tip: Copper recycling: ~85% energy saving vs extraction. Avoids acid mine drainage, habitat loss, and CO2 from smelting. Copper is infinitely recyclable.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Why is pure copper used for electrical wiring rather than a copper alloy?
option_a: Alloys are always more brittle
option_b: Pure copper has higher electrical conductivity because the regular atomic structure allows electrons to flow more freely; alloy atoms scatter electrons, reducing conductivity
option_c: Alloys corrode faster than pure copper
option_d: Pure copper is always cheaper than alloys
explanation: Alloying atoms disrupt the regular crystal structure, scattering conduction electrons and reducing electrical conductivity. Pure copper regular structure allows maximum electron flow.
correction_tip: Pure metals: better electrical conductivity (regular structure). Alloys: harder but lower conductivity. Pure Cu used for wiring; brass (Cu+Zn) used for fittings.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the role of adding alum (aluminium sulfate) during water treatment?
option_a: To kill bacteria in the water
option_b: Alum produces Al(OH)3 floc that traps fine suspended particles, making them heavy enough to settle out
option_c: To remove dissolved salts from the water
option_d: To adjust the pH of water only
explanation: Alum (Al2(SO4)3) dissolved in water produces Al(OH)3 which forms a gelatinous floc. This traps fine clay particles and some microorganisms, allowing them to settle in sedimentation tanks.
correction_tip: Alum coagulation: Al3+ + 3OH- -> Al(OH)3 floc. Sticky floc traps fine particles -> settles. Makes filtration more effective.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: Evaluate the trade-off between using bioplastics versus recycled petroleum-based plastics.
option_a: Bioplastics are always better than recycled plastics
option_b: Bioplastics use renewable plant sources and may be biodegradable but require agricultural land and water. Recycled plastics use existing material avoiding new resource extraction but quality decreases. LCA shows mixed results depending on assumptions.
option_c: Recycled petroleum plastics are always better
option_d: There is no difference between bioplastics and recycled plastics
explanation: Bioplastics pros: renewable, biodegradable if composted. Cons: land/water/fertiliser use, may compete with food. Recycled plastics pros: diverts waste, less new resource extraction. Cons: downcycling quality loss.
correction_tip: Bioplastic vs recycled: complex LCA. Bioplastic: renewable but land/energy use. Recycled: diverts waste but quality decreases. Neither clearly superior - depends on use case.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: What is the difference between closed-loop and open-loop recycling?
option_a: Both terms mean the same thing
option_b: Closed-loop: material recycled back into same product (e.g. aluminium can to can). Open-loop: material downcycled into lower-value product (e.g. plastic bottle to fleece). Closed-loop is more sustainable as quality is maintained.
option_c: Open-loop recycling is always better
option_d: Closed-loop only applies to glass recycling
explanation: Closed-loop recycling maintains material quality indefinitely. Open-loop downcycling loses quality with each cycle. Aluminium and glass can be closed-loop; most plastics are open-loop.
correction_tip: Closed-loop (Al can->can): same quality forever. Open-loop (plastic bottle->fleece->landfill): quality degrades. Aluminium and glass: closed-loop possible. Most plastics: open-loop (downcycling).

subject: Chemistry
question_text: The green steel industry aims to use hydrogen instead of coke to reduce iron ore. Evaluate this approach.
option_a: Green steel uses the same process as conventional steel
option_b: Green steel uses H2 to reduce iron ore: Fe2O3 + 3H2 -> 2Fe + 3H2O (water not CO2 produced). Highly sustainable if H2 is from renewable electrolysis. Currently more expensive and H2 supply is limited but pilot plants are operating.
option_c: Green steel produces the same CO2 as conventional steel
option_d: Hydrogen cannot reduce iron oxide
explanation: Green steel: Fe2O3 + 3H2 -> 2Fe + 3H2O. No CO2 produced (only water). Steel industry accounts for 7-9% global CO2. Green H2 from renewable electrolysis makes this near zero-carbon. HYBRIT project in Sweden is a real example.
correction_tip: Green steel: Fe2O3 + H2 -> Fe + H2O instead of Fe2O3 + CO -> Fe + CO2. No CO2 if H2 is green. HYBRIT (Sweden) = world first commercial green steel. Critical for industrial decarbonisation.

subject: Chemistry
question_text: How does industrial symbiosis contribute to sustainable resource use? Give an example.
option_a: Industrial symbiosis is theoretical with no practical examples
option_b: Industrial symbiosis: waste from one industry becomes input for another. Example: Kalundborg, Denmark - power station waste heat heats a fish farm; fly ash goes to cement manufacture; steam goes to a pharmaceutical company. Reduces resource use and waste across multiple industries.
option_c: Industrial symbiosis only applies to water recycling
option_d: Industrial symbiosis requires all companies to merge into one
explanation: Kalundborg Industrial Symbiosis: power station flue gas gypsum goes to wallboard factory. Steam from power station serves pharmaceutical/oil refinery. Fly ash goes to cement. Network reduces waste and resource extraction.
correction_tip: Industrial symbiosis: waste of one industry = resource for another. Kalundborg most famous example. Reduces both costs and environmental impacts. Also called circular industrial ecology.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a contact force?
option_a: Gravity
option_b: Magnetism
option_c: Friction
option_d: Electrostatic force
explanation: Friction is a contact force because it only acts when two surfaces are touching. Gravity, magnetism and electrostatic forces are non-contact forces.
correction_tip: Contact forces require physical contact between objects; non-contact forces act at a distance.

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the unit of force?
option_a: Joule
option_b: Watt
option_c: Newton
option_d: Pascal
explanation: Force is measured in Newtons (N), named after Isaac Newton.
correction_tip: Remember: Newton = kg m/s^2. Do not confuse with Joule (energy) or Watt (power).

subject: Physics
question_text: An object has a mass of 5 kg. What is its weight on Earth where g = 10 N/kg?
option_a: 2 N
correction_tip: Use W = mg. Mass is in kg, g = 10 N/kg on Earth, weight is in Newtons.

subject: Physics
question_text: What does a resultant force of zero mean for a stationary object?
option_a: It accelerates
option_b: It remains stationary
option_c: It moves in a circle
option_d: It decelerates
explanation: If the resultant force is zero and the object is stationary, it remains stationary (Newton's 1st Law).
correction_tip: Zero resultant force means no change in motion - stationary objects stay still, moving objects continue at constant velocity.

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the formula for calculating speed?
option_a: speed = distance x time
option_b: speed = distance / time
option_c: speed = time / distance
option_d: speed = force / mass
explanation: Speed = distance / time (v = s/t). It is measured in metres per second (m/s).
correction_tip: Remember the formula triangle: distance = speed x time. Cover what you want to find.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following best describes a scalar quantity?
option_a: Has magnitude and direction
option_b: Has magnitude only
option_c: Has direction only
option_d: Has no measurable value
explanation: Scalar quantities have magnitude (size) only. Examples include speed, mass, and temperature.
correction_tip: Scalars have size only; vectors have both size and direction. Speed is scalar, velocity is vector.

subject: Physics
question_text: A car travels 120 m in 10 seconds. What is its average speed?
option_b: 12 m/s
explanation: Speed = distance / time = 120 / 10 = 12 m/s.
correction_tip: Divide distance by time to get speed. Check units carefully.

subject: Physics
question_text: What does a horizontal line on a distance-time graph represent?
option_a: Constant speed
option_b: Acceleration
option_c: The object is stationary
option_d: Deceleration
explanation: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the distance is not changing, so the object is stationary.
correction_tip: Slope on a distance-time graph = speed. No slope = no movement.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction?
option_a: Newton's 1st Law
option_b: Newton's 2nd Law
option_c: Newton's 3rd Law
option_d: Hooke's Law
explanation: Newton's 3rd Law states that forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different objects.
correction_tip: 3rd Law pairs act on DIFFERENT objects. The forces are equal in size but opposite in direction.

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the difference between mass and weight?
option_a: Mass is measured in Newtons; weight in kg
option_b: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the gravitational force on that mass
option_c: They are the same thing
option_d: Mass changes with gravity; weight does not
explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (kg). Weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass (N).
correction_tip: Mass is constant everywhere. Weight changes depending on gravitational field strength.

subject: Physics
question_text: An object at rest on a table has two forces acting on it: weight downward and normal reaction upward. What can you conclude?
option_a: The object is accelerating upward
option_b: The forces are unbalanced
option_c: The resultant force is zero
option_d: Weight is greater than normal reaction
explanation: Since the object is at rest, the forces must be balanced and the resultant force is zero.
correction_tip: Balanced forces (resultant = 0) mean no change in motion.

subject: Physics
question_text: What does a steeper gradient on a distance-time graph indicate?
option_a: Slower speed
option_b: Greater speed
option_c: Negative acceleration
option_d: Constant acceleration
explanation: A steeper gradient on a distance-time graph means the object covers more distance per unit time, so it is moving faster.
correction_tip: Gradient = speed on a d-t graph. Steeper = faster.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of these is a non-contact force?
option_a: Air resistance
option_b: Tension
option_c: Normal reaction
option_d: Gravity
explanation: Gravity acts at a distance without objects needing to touch. The others require contact.
correction_tip: Non-contact forces: gravity, magnetism, electrostatic. Contact forces: friction, tension, normal reaction, air resistance.

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the unit of acceleration?
option_a: m/s
option_b: m/s^2
option_c: N/kg
option_d: kg m/s
explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, measured in metres per second squared (m/s^2).
correction_tip: Acceleration = change in velocity / time. Units = m/s divided by s = m/s^2.

subject: Physics
question_text: A free body diagram shows the forces acting on an object. If an object has 30 N to the right and 10 N to the left, what is the resultant force?
option_a: 40 N to the right
option_b: 20 N to the left
option_c: 20 N to the right
option_d: 30 N to the right
explanation: Resultant = 30 - 10 = 20 N in the direction of the larger force (to the right).
correction_tip: For forces along the same line, subtract smaller from larger and use the direction of the larger force.

subject: Physics
question_text: Stopping distance is made up of which two distances?
option_a: Reaction distance and impact distance
option_b: Thinking distance and braking distance
option_c: Speed distance and time distance
option_d: Initial distance and final distance
explanation: Stopping distance = thinking distance (distance travelled during reaction time) + braking distance (distance during braking).
correction_tip: Thinking distance depends on reaction time; braking distance depends on speed, road conditions and brakes.

subject: Physics
question_text: A resultant force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg object. What is the acceleration of the object?
explanation: F = ma, so a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s^2.
correction_tip: Rearrange F = ma to a = F/m. Ensure units are consistent (N, kg, m/s^2).

subject: Physics
question_text: A spring with spring constant 200 N/m is extended by 0.05 m. What is the force applied?
option_d: 4 N
explanation: F = ke = 200 x 0.05 = 10 N (Hooke's Law).
correction_tip: Hooke's Law: F = ke where k is spring constant (N/m) and e is extension (m).

subject: Physics
question_text: How much work is done when a 500 N force moves an object 3 m in the direction of the force?
explanation: Work done = Force x distance = 500 x 3 = 1500 J.
correction_tip: W = Fs. Work done is in Joules. Distance must be in the direction of the force.

subject: Physics
question_text: A velocity-time graph shows a straight line with positive gradient. What does this represent?
option_a: Constant velocity
option_b: Uniform deceleration
option_c: Uniform acceleration
option_d: Zero velocity
explanation: A straight line with positive gradient on a v-t graph means velocity increases uniformly, which is uniform acceleration.
correction_tip: Gradient of v-t graph = acceleration. Positive gradient = acceleration; negative = deceleration.

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the pressure exerted by a force of 100 N over an area of 0.5 m^2?
option_a: 50 Pa
option_b: 200 Pa
explanation: Pressure = Force / Area = 100 / 0.5 = 200 Pa.
correction_tip: p = F/A. Pressure is in Pascals (Pa = N/m^2). Smaller area = greater pressure for same force.

subject: Physics
question_text: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration?
correction_tip: Use a = (v - u) / t. v is final velocity, u is initial velocity.

subject: Physics
question_text: What is the momentum of a 3 kg object moving at 8 m/s?
option_a: 24 kg m/s
option_b: 2.67 kg m/s
option_c: 11 kg m/s
option_d: 0.375 kg m/s
explanation: Momentum p = mv = 3 x 8 = 24 kg m/s.
correction_tip: p = mv. Units are kg m/s. Momentum is a vector quantity.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which factor does NOT affect thinking distance when stopping a vehicle?
option_a: Speed of the vehicle
option_b: Condition of the tyres
option_c: Reaction time of the driver
option_d: Tiredness of the driver
explanation: Tyre condition affects braking distance, not thinking distance. Thinking distance depends on reaction time, which is affected by speed, tiredness, alcohol, and distractions.
correction_tip: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time. Anything affecting reaction time affects thinking distance.

subject: Physics
