question_text: Why can antibiotics not be used to treat influenza (flu)?
option_a: Antibiotics are too expensive for flu treatment
option_b: Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only target bacterial cell structures (not present in viruses)
option_c: Antibiotics cause flu symptoms to worsen
option_d: Flu bacteria are always antibiotic-resistant
explanation: Antibiotics work by targeting structures specific to bacteria (cell walls, ribosomes). Viruses lack these structures and reproduce inside host cells, so antibiotics have no target and cannot work against viral infections like flu.
correction_tip: Antibiotics = antibacterial only. Viruses: no cell wall, replicate inside host cells using host machinery. Antivirals (e.g. oseltamivir/Tamiflu for flu) exist but are different drugs. Overusing antibiotics for viral infections contributes to resistance.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain how antibiotic resistance develops in bacteria.
option_a: Bacteria choose to become resistant when exposed to antibiotics
option_b: Random mutations in bacteria can produce individuals resistant to antibiotics. When antibiotics are used, non-resistant bacteria are killed but resistant ones survive and reproduce, passing on resistant genes (natural selection). Overuse and incomplete courses of antibiotics accelerate this process.
option_c: Bacteria inject DNA into patients making them unable to produce antibiotics
option_d: Antibiotic resistance is caused by patients sharing their antibiotics
explanation: Antibiotic resistance is an example of natural selection: mutation → variation in resistance → selection pressure (antibiotic) → survival of resistant strains → reproduction and spread of resistance gene. MRSA is a famous example.
correction_tip: Resistance mechanism: random mutation → some resistant → antibiotics kill sensitive → resistant survive + reproduce → resistance spreads. Also via plasmid transfer between bacteria. Prevention: complete courses, prescribe only when needed, new antibiotic development.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe the process of phagocytosis.
option_a: Phagocytes produce antibodies that neutralise pathogens
option_b: Phagocytes detect pathogens via chemical signals, engulf them by surrounding with their membrane forming a phagosome, then fuse with lysosomes containing enzymes that digest and destroy the pathogen.
option_c: Phagocytosis involves T-cells injecting venom into pathogens
option_d: Phagocytes release chemicals that explode pathogens from a distance
explanation: Phagocytosis: 1) Phagocyte detects pathogen (attracted by chemicals). 2) Membrane extends around pathogen forming a phagosome. 3) Lysosomes (containing digestive enzymes) fuse with phagosome. 4) Enzymes digest the pathogen.
correction_tip: Phagocytosis steps: 1) detect pathogen 2) engulf (form phagosome) 3) lysosomes fuse 4) enzymes digest pathogen 5) debris expelled. Non-specific (attacks any foreign body). Phagocytes: neutrophils and macrophages.

subject: Biology
question_text: How does the skin act as a defence against pathogens?
option_a: The skin produces antibodies that kill pathogens on contact
option_b: Unbroken skin is a physical barrier; it is also slightly acidic and secretes antimicrobial oils. Cuts allow pathogen entry which is why they must be covered. Sebum from sebaceous glands and sweat (slightly acidic) add chemical defence.
option_c: The skin only defends against bacteria, not viruses
option_d: Skin colour determines effectiveness of the immune barrier
explanation: Intact skin: physical barrier impenetrable to most pathogens. Skin secretions: sebum (antimicrobial lipids) and sweat (acidic pH, lysozyme) add chemical defence. Breaks in skin (cuts, burns) bypass this first line.
correction_tip: Skin defences: physical barrier (unbroken), slightly acidic surface, sebum (antimicrobial), sweat contains lysozyme. Cilia and mucus: respiratory barrier. Stomach acid: kills swallowed pathogens. All are non-specific first-line defences.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why does having a disease once often provide immunity against future infection by the same pathogen?
option_a: The pathogen is permanently eliminated from the body so cannot cause disease again
option_b: The first infection stimulates B-lymphocytes to produce antibodies and form long-lived memory cells. On second exposure to the same antigen, memory cells rapidly produce large quantities of antibodies before the pathogen can multiply to cause symptoms.
option_c: The body becomes physically immune after fever burns the pathogen away
option_d: Antibodies remain in the blood indefinitely and kill pathogens immediately
explanation: Immunological memory: primary immune response creates memory B-cells (and T-cells). Secondary response is faster and produces more antibodies — the pathogen is eliminated before symptoms develop. This is the basis of vaccination.
correction_tip: Immunological memory: 1st infection → memory cells formed. 2nd exposure → rapid secondary response (faster, stronger). Memory cells are long-lived (sometimes lifetime). Natural immunity vs vaccine-induced immunity — both create memory cells.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe how the MMR vaccine provides protection against measles, mumps, and rubella.
option_a: The MMR vaccine contains three separate doses of antibiotics
option_b: MMR contains live attenuated (weakened) strains of measles, mumps, and rubella viruses. These stimulate immune responses producing memory cells for all three diseases without causing illness. If exposed to any of these viruses later, the rapid immune response prevents disease.
option_c: The MMR vaccine contains antigens from only one disease at a time
option_d: MMR provides only temporary protection for 6 months
explanation: MMR is a combined live-attenuated vaccine. Weakened viruses replicate slightly but cannot cause disease in healthy people. They stimulate strong, long-lasting immune memory for measles, mumps, and rubella.
correction_tip: MMR: live attenuated (weakened) vaccine. Provides long-lasting immunity. Given at ~12 months and ~3 years. Herd immunity requires ~95% coverage. Debunked myths: no link to autism (Wakefield's study was fraudulent and retracted).

subject: Biology
question_text: What is herd immunity and why is a high vaccination rate important to achieve it?
option_a: Herd immunity means every individual is immune after vaccination
option_b: Herd immunity occurs when such a large proportion of the population is immune that the pathogen cannot spread effectively, protecting even unvaccinated individuals. High coverage is needed because if too many people are susceptible, chains of transmission can persist.
option_c: Herd immunity only applies to animal diseases, not human ones
option_d: Herd immunity requires 100% vaccination to work
explanation: Herd immunity breaks transmission chains: immune individuals do not pass infection to others, protecting vulnerable people (too young, immunocompromised) who cannot be vaccinated. Threshold varies by disease (measles ~95%).
correction_tip: Herd immunity: enough immune individuals (vaccinated or recovered) that pathogen cannot find susceptible hosts to spread. Protects those who cannot be vaccinated (newborns, immunocompromised). Threshold varies: measles ~95%, polio ~80-85%.

subject: Biology
question_text: How does HIV cause AIDS?
option_a: HIV directly destroys all red blood cells
option_b: HIV attacks and destroys T-helper lymphocytes (CD4 cells) which coordinate the immune response. As T-cell count falls, the immune system becomes progressively unable to fight infections. AIDS is diagnosed when the count falls below 200 cells/mm³ and opportunistic infections develop.
option_c: HIV produces toxins that attack the liver
option_d: HIV only affects people with weak muscles
explanation: T-helper cells coordinate both antibody production (B-cells) and cell-killing (cytotoxic T-cells). Destroying them collapses the adaptive immune response. People with AIDS die from infections that a healthy immune system would easily control.
correction_tip: HIV targets: T-helper cells (CD4+ lymphocytes). Progressive destruction → weakened adaptive immunity → AIDS. Opportunistic infections (TB, pneumonia, candida) cause death, not HIV directly. Antiretrovirals suppress viral replication, maintaining T-cell count.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe the difference between a vaccine and an antiviral drug, using flu as an example.
option_a: Vaccines and antivirals work in the same way; only the route of administration differs
option_b: A flu vaccine (containing inactivated or attenuated flu virus) is given before infection to stimulate memory cells, preventing disease. An antiviral drug (e.g. oseltamivir/Tamiflu) is taken after infection begins; it inhibits viral replication enzymes to reduce severity and duration but does not prevent infection.
option_c: Antivirals can replace vaccines for all viral diseases
option_d: Vaccines treat disease; antivirals prevent it
explanation: Vaccine = prophylactic (before exposure, stimulates immunity). Antiviral = therapeutic (after infection, reduces replication). Flu vaccines must be updated annually due to antigenic variation in the flu virus.
correction_tip: Vaccine: prophylactic, stimulates immune memory before infection. Antiviral: therapeutic, reduces viral replication after infection. Flu vaccine updated annually (antigenic drift changes surface antigens). Tamiflu: neuraminidase inhibitor, reduces severity if taken early.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why is there no effective antibiotic treatment for tuberculosis that works in a single short course?
option_a: Tuberculosis is caused by a virus so antibiotics have no effect at all
option_b: Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly and can lie dormant inside macrophages, making it hard to kill. It rapidly develops antibiotic resistance. Treatment requires multiple antibiotics over 6 months to kill all bacteria, including dormant cells, and prevent resistance.
option_c: Antibiotics cannot cross the lung wall to reach the bacteria
option_d: TB bacteria have no ribosomes so antibiotic targets are absent
explanation: TB bacteria are slow-growing, can become dormant inside immune cells, and are naturally resistant to many antibiotics. Multiple-drug regimens (isoniazid, rifampicin) over 6 months prevent resistance emergence and clear dormant bacteria.
correction_tip: TB treatment: 6 months, 4 antibiotics initially (2 months) then 2 antibiotics (4 months). Reasons for length: slow growth, dormant bacteria, resistance prevention. MDR-TB (multi-drug resistant TB) is a serious global health problem.

subject: Biology
question_text: What specific adaptations help pathogens spread between hosts successfully?
option_a: All pathogens use exactly the same methods to spread
option_b: Pathogens are adapted to their transmission route: respiratory pathogens replicate in airways producing many particles expelled in droplets; gut pathogens survive stomach acid; vector-borne pathogens survive in the mosquito gut; sexually transmitted pathogens are fragile outside the body but transmitted efficiently during contact.
option_c: Pathogens have no specific adaptations — they spread by chance only
option_d: All pathogens spread only by direct contact
explanation: Each pathogen is evolutionarily adapted to its transmission route. Influenza produces millions of virions in respiratory cells, spreads in droplets. Cholera bacteria produce massive diarrhoea to contaminate water supplies. Malaria Plasmodium develops specific forms in mosquito salivary glands.
correction_tip: Transmission adaptations: influenza (respiratory droplets, high viral load in throat), cholera (toxin causes diarrhoea → water contamination), HIV (immune evasion, long latent period), malaria (sporozoites in mosquito saliva). Adapted for efficient host-to-host transfer.

subject: Biology
question_text: How can the spread of communicable diseases be reduced in a school setting?
option_a: By providing antibiotics to all students as a preventative measure
option_b: By frequent handwashing (removes pathogen from skin), covering coughs/sneezes (reduces droplet spread), staying home when ill (prevents contact), good ventilation (dilutes airborne pathogens), and vaccination programmes.
option_c: By using antiviral sprays on all surfaces continuously
option_d: By isolating all students in separate rooms permanently
explanation: Public health measures reduce transmission: handwashing (interrupts contact/faecal-oral routes), respiratory hygiene (reduces droplet spread), isolation when ill, vaccination for preventable diseases, cleaning surfaces.
correction_tip: Disease control: handwashing (contact/faecal-oral), respiratory hygiene (droplets), isolation (prevent spread from case), vaccination (herd immunity), vector control (malaria: nets/insecticide), clean water (cholera). Match control to transmission route.

subject: Biology
question_text: What are monoclonal antibodies and how are they produced?
option_a: Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies found naturally in high concentrations in blood
option_b: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies produced from a single clone of B-cells. A mouse is immunised with a target antigen; its B-lymphocytes are fused with myeloma (cancer) cells to produce hybridoma cells that divide rapidly and produce unlimited identical antibodies.
option_c: Monoclonal antibodies are produced by bacteria in fermenters
option_d: Monoclonal antibodies can only be produced from human cells
explanation: Hybridoma technology: immunise mouse → isolate B-cells → fuse with myeloma cells → hybridoma cells → clone → produce identical monoclonal antibodies. These are highly specific to one antigen.
correction_tip: Monoclonal antibodies: made by hybridoma cells (B-cell + myeloma fusion). Identical, specific to one antigen. Uses: pregnancy tests, cancer diagnosis/treatment (e.g. Herceptin), COVID lateral flow tests. GCSE: understand production steps.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain the concept of antigenic variation in influenza virus and why it makes vaccine development difficult.
option_a: Antigenic variation means the flu virus produces toxins that change composition each year
option_b: Influenza viruses mutate rapidly, changing the structure of surface antigens (haemagglutinin and neuraminidase). Memory cells produced against previous strains no longer recognise new antigenic variants, making annual vaccination necessary. Major antigenic shifts (gene reassortment) can produce pandemic strains to which no population has immunity.
option_c: Antigenic variation only occurs in bacteria, not viruses
option_d: The flu vaccine does not need updating because flu antigens never change
explanation: Antigenic drift: small gradual mutations in H and N antigens requiring annual vaccine updates. Antigenic shift: sudden major change through reassortment of gene segments (e.g. swine+human+bird flu) producing novel pandemic strains.
correction_tip: Antigenic drift: gradual mutation of surface antigens (HA/NA) → annual vaccine needed. Antigenic shift: major reassortment of gene segments → pandemic potential (1918 Spanish flu, 2009 H1N1). Both mean existing immunity may not protect against new variants.

subject: Biology
question_text: How do monoclonal antibodies work as cancer treatments, and what advantages do they have over traditional chemotherapy?
option_a: Monoclonal antibodies are used instead of all surgical treatments
option_b: Monoclonal antibodies (e.g. Herceptin) bind specifically to antigens on cancer cells but not normal cells. They can be used alone to mark cells for immune attack, block growth signals, or be conjugated with toxins/radioactive labels to deliver targeted treatment. Advantage over chemotherapy: greater specificity means less damage to healthy cells and fewer side effects.
option_c: Monoclonal antibodies are injected into tumours and physically destroy them
option_d: Monoclonal antibodies only work for blood cancers
explanation: Targeted therapy: monoclonal antibodies bind cancer-specific antigens (e.g. HER2 on certain breast cancers). Mechanisms: block growth factor receptors, trigger apoptosis, recruit immune cells, or deliver cytotoxic drugs to tumour cells. More precise than chemotherapy.
correction_tip: Monoclonal antibody cancer therapy: Herceptin (Trastuzumab) targets HER2+ breast cancer. Advantages: specific (less normal cell damage), fewer side effects than chemo. Modes: block receptors, immune activation, radioimmunotherapy, antibody-drug conjugates.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe the roles of B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes in the adaptive immune response.
option_a: Both B and T lymphocytes carry out phagocytosis of pathogens
option_b: B-lymphocytes: mature in bone marrow, recognise specific antigens, differentiate into plasma cells (produce antibodies) and memory B-cells. T-lymphocytes: mature in thymus, helper T-cells activate B-cells and phagocytes, cytotoxic T-cells kill infected host cells, memory T-cells persist.
option_c: T-lymphocytes produce antibodies; B-lymphocytes kill infected cells
option_d: Lymphocytes only act in lymph nodes and do not enter the bloodstream
explanation: Adaptive immunity involves both cellular (T-cell) and humoral (B-cell/antibody) responses. Helper T-cells coordinate the response; cytotoxic T-cells kill infected cells; B-cells produce antibodies. Memory cells of both types provide long-term immunity.
correction_tip: B-cells: bone marrow maturation, antibody production (plasma cells), memory B-cells. T-cells: thymus maturation. Helper T (CD4): coordinate response. Cytotoxic T (CD8): kill infected cells. Memory T: rapid secondary response. Both arms work together.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain the stages in the development of a new drug from initial discovery to patient use, including why this process takes many years.
option_a: New drugs can be approved and used in patients within weeks of discovery
option_b: Drug development stages: 1) Discovery/screening (potential compounds identified). 2) Preclinical testing (cell/animal testing for toxicity and efficacy). 3) Phase I clinical trial (small group, safety). 4) Phase II (larger group, optimal dose). 5) Phase III (large randomised controlled trial, efficacy vs placebo). 6) Regulatory approval. 7) Phase IV (post-market surveillance). Process takes 10-15 years due to safety requirements.
option_c: Clinical trials are optional if a drug proves effective in animal testing
option_d: Drugs only need one stage of testing before patient use
explanation: Rigorous testing is required to ensure drugs are safe and effective. Each stage eliminates unsuitable candidates. Phase III RCTs provide the gold-standard evidence. The long timeline reflects the complexity of establishing safety and efficacy in humans.
correction_tip: Drug development: discovery → preclinical (cells+animals) → Phase I (safety, n=~20) → Phase II (dose/efficacy, n=~100s) → Phase III (RCT, n=~1000s) → approval → Phase IV (surveillance). Total: 10-15 years, ~£1 billion. Most candidates fail during trials.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe two uses of monoclonal antibodies in diagnosis, with specific examples.
option_a: Monoclonal antibodies cannot be used for diagnosis
option_b: 1) Pregnancy tests: antibodies on test strip bind to hCG hormone in urine; labelled secondary antibody produces visible line. 2) Cancer diagnosis: radioactively or fluorescently labelled antibodies injected into patient bind specifically to tumour antigens allowing imaging of tumour location/size. Also: ELISA tests for infectious diseases (HIV, COVID lateral flow tests).
option_c: Diagnostic uses of monoclonal antibodies are still theoretical
option_d: Monoclonal antibodies diagnose diseases by repairing damaged cells
explanation: Monoclonal antibody diagnostics exploit their specificity. Pregnancy tests (hCG detection), cancer imaging (antibodies carry imaging labels to tumours), infectious disease tests (lateral flow for COVID). The antibody binds only its specific antigen.
correction_tip: Diagnostic uses: pregnancy test (anti-hCG antibody), cancer imaging (labelled antibody → tumour), HIV/COVID tests (lateral flow ELISA). Principle: antibody binds specific antigen only → confirms presence. Fast, specific, sensitive. No current treatment function in the test itself.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why does the global spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria pose such a serious public health challenge? Include two specific mechanisms of resistance.
option_a: Antibiotic resistance is not a serious problem because new antibiotics are easily developed
option_b: Resistance mechanisms include: (1) bacteria produce enzymes (e.g. beta-lactamase) that destroy the antibiotic; (2) bacteria mutate their target sites so the antibiotic cannot bind. Resistance genes spread rapidly via plasmid transfer between bacteria (horizontal gene transfer). The pipeline for new antibiotics is extremely limited, and resistant infections (e.g. MRSA, XDR-TB) already cause significant mortality. Global travel spreads resistant strains internationally.
option_c: Only one resistance mechanism exists: bacteria become immune after repeated exposure
option_d: Antibiotic resistance can be solved simply by increasing antibiotic doses
explanation: Beta-lactamases inactivate penicillin-class antibiotics. Target site mutations (e.g. altered penicillin-binding proteins in MRSA) prevent antibiotic binding. Plasmid transfer: one bacterium can give resistance to another, even across species. The antibiotic pipeline is thin.
correction_tip: Resistance mechanisms: enzyme inactivation (beta-lactamase destroys penicillin), target mutation (MRSA altered PBP), efflux pumps (pump antibiotic out), reduced permeability. Plasmid transfer: fast cross-species spread. Solutions: new drug development, antibiotic stewardship, phage therapy.

subject: Biology
question_text: Compare the primary and secondary immune responses in terms of speed, antibody levels, and the cells responsible.
option_a: Primary and secondary responses are identical in speed and antibody production
option_b: Primary response: 1-2 weeks to produce significant antibodies (slow as naive B-cells must be selected and proliferate); lower peak antibody level; some memory cells formed. Secondary response (re-exposure): within 1-3 days, faster and 10-100× higher antibody peak due to large pool of memory B-cells rapidly differentiating into plasma cells. This is why recovery from re-infection is fast and often symptom-free.
option_c: Secondary response is slower because the immune system is exhausted from the first response
option_d: Primary response always causes severe disease; secondary never causes any symptoms
explanation: Memory B-cells (and T-cells) formed during primary response proliferate rapidly on re-exposure. The secondary response is both faster and produces more antibodies — disease is prevented before symptoms develop. This is the biological basis of vaccination.
correction_tip: Primary: slow (1-2 weeks), lower antibody peak, naive B-cells recruited. Secondary: fast (1-3 days), high antibody peak, memory B-cells activated. Graph: compare curves. Vaccination mimics primary response so real infection gets secondary response.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain how the malaria parasite evades the human immune system.
option_a: Plasmodium produces antiviral chemicals that destroy immune cells
option_b: Plasmodium evades immunity by: (1) hiding inside liver cells and red blood cells (intracellular, hidden from antibodies); (2) rapidly changing surface antigens (antigenic variation), so antibodies made against one variant do not recognise the next; (3) inhibiting immune cell signalling. This makes both natural immunity and vaccine development very difficult.
option_c: Malaria is too small for the immune system to detect
option_d: The mosquito destroys antibodies before injecting Plasmodium
explanation: Plasmodium falciparum: intracellular life cycle (liver then RBCs) hides from antibodies; rapid antigenic variation of surface proteins (e.g. PfEMP1) allows immune evasion; immune suppression mechanisms. This is why immunity to malaria is incomplete and brief.
correction_tip: Plasmodium immune evasion: intracellular (hidden from antibodies), antigenic variation (PfEMP1 variants), immune modulation. Incomplete natural immunity: people in endemic areas develop partial immunity after many infections. This is why malaria vaccine development is very challenging (RTS,S vaccine only ~40% effective).

subject: Biology
question_text: What ethical issues surround the use of animals in preclinical drug testing?
option_a: There are no ethical issues with animal testing as animals cannot feel pain
option_b: Animals are used to test drug toxicity and efficacy before human trials. Ethical concerns: animal suffering and right to life (particularly for sentient species); animal physiology may not accurately predict human response (e.g. thalidomide was safe in some animal species but caused birth defects in humans). Justified by: preventing harm to humans from untested drugs; legal requirements. Minimised by: 3Rs framework (Replace with cell/computer models, Reduce numbers, Refine procedures to minimise suffering).
option_c: Animal testing always perfectly predicts human drug responses
option_d: Animal testing has been entirely replaced by computer models
explanation: The 3Rs framework (NC3Rs): Replace animals with alternatives (cell cultures, organ-on-a-chip, computer models) where possible; Reduce numbers; Refine methods to minimise suffering. Animal testing remains legally required for many drugs but is progressively being supplemented by alternatives.
correction_tip: Animal testing ethics: for (human safety, legal requirement), against (animal suffering, poor predictivity). 3Rs: Replace (alternatives), Reduce (fewer animals), Refine (less suffering). Thalidomide example: appeared safe in some animals but caused limb defects in humans.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe how the respiratory system acts as a barrier against pathogens.
option_a: The respiratory system has no specific defences — all pathogens pass directly into the lungs
option_b: The trachea and bronchi are lined with mucus-secreting goblet cells and ciliated epithelial cells. Mucus traps pathogens; cilia beat continuously moving mucus (and trapped pathogens) upward toward the throat (mucociliary escalator) where it is swallowed and destroyed by stomach acid. Macrophages in alveoli phagocytose any pathogens reaching that far.
option_c: Stomach acid flows into the lungs to kill pathogens
option_d: The trachea produces antibodies that kill airborne pathogens
explanation: Mucociliary clearance: goblet cells secrete mucus trapping pathogens/particles; ciliated cells beat rhythmically (~1000 beats/min) to move mucus to pharynx; swallowed mucus is digested in stomach. Smoking paralyses cilia, impairing this defence.
correction_tip: Respiratory defences: mucus (traps pathogens), cilia (move mucus upward - mucociliary escalator), alveolar macrophages (phagocytose). Smoking: destroys cilia → mucus accumulates → increased infection risk → smoker's cough. CF: thick mucus blocks escalator.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why do immunocompromised patients (e.g. those on immunosuppressants after organ transplant) need to be protected from infections that healthy people easily resist?
option_a: Immunosuppressants only affect memory cells, not the ability to fight new infections
option_b: Immunosuppressants suppress the adaptive immune response to prevent organ rejection. This reduces T and B-cell activity, weakening defence against pathogens. Opportunistic infections (e.g. Pneumocystis pneumonia, CMV) that a healthy immune system would easily clear can become life-threatening. Such patients need prophylactic antibiotics/antivirals and avoid live vaccines.
option_c: Immunocompromised patients have stronger innate immunity to compensate
option_d: Organ transplant patients only need protection for the first week
explanation: Immunosuppressants (e.g. cyclosporine) prevent rejection by suppressing T-cells. This leaves patients vulnerable to infections normally controlled by T-cell immunity. Opportunistic pathogens (Toxoplasma, CMV, fungal infections) are dangerous in this state.
correction_tip: Immunosuppression: needed to prevent organ rejection but compromises immunity. Opportunistic infections: caused by organisms harmless to healthy people. Examples: PCP (fungal), CMV (viral), Toxoplasma. Management: prophylactic antibiotics/antivirals, avoid crowds/live vaccines, regular monitoring.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain how the discovery of penicillin by Fleming was followed by its development into a usable medicine, and what this illustrates about drug development.
option_a: Fleming immediately distributed penicillin as a medicine after observing its effect in 1928
option_b: Fleming observed that Penicillium mould killed Staphylococcus bacteria on a contaminated plate in 1928. However, he could not purify or produce it in sufficient quantities. A decade later, Florey and Chain purified penicillin, tested it in mice (1940), then in humans (1941). Mass production was achieved during WWII. This illustrates that discovery does not equal medicine — development requires purification, safety testing, production scale-up, and clinical trials.
option_c: Penicillin was synthesised chemically in a laboratory before any clinical testing
option_d: Fleming himself conducted all clinical trials and approved penicillin for use
explanation: Fleming's serendipitous observation → Florey and Chain's development. The 10-year gap illustrates the complexity of going from natural source to usable medicine. All three shared the Nobel Prize 1945. It established the template for antibiotic development.
correction_tip: Penicillin history: Fleming 1928 (observation), Florey+Chain 1940-41 (purification + testing), WWII mass production. Nobel Prize 1945 (all three). Discovery ≠ medicine. Shows: need purification, toxicity testing, clinical trials, manufacturing scale-up. Serendipity + scientific follow-through.

subject: Biology
question_text: Evaluate the challenges of developing an effective vaccine against HIV, considering the virus's specific properties.
option_a: An HIV vaccine has been available since the 1990s with high efficacy
option_b: HIV vaccine development faces extraordinary challenges: (1) HIV integrates into host genome (provirus) making complete elimination impossible; (2) extreme antigenic variation (HIV mutates its surface proteins rapidly, including gp120 which antibodies must target); (3) HIV destroys the very T-helper cells needed to mount an immune response; (4) no natural clearance of HIV occurs in any human, making it hard to identify protective immune responses to replicate. Despite 40 years of research, no effective vaccine exists.
option_c: HIV vaccines fail only because of lack of funding for research
option_d: HIV is resistant to all antigens used in vaccines
explanation: The combination of genomic integration, extreme mutation rate (high-fidelity reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading), immune evasion, and targeting of the cells needed for immunity makes HIV uniquely challenging. Novel approaches (broadly neutralising antibodies, mRNA vaccines) are in trials.
correction_tip: HIV vaccine challenges: viral integration (not cleared), extreme mutation (no proofreading by reverse transcriptase), destroys helper T-cells (needed for vaccine response), no natural clearance (no model for protective immunity), variable across subtypes. Contrast: smallpox (stable antigens, cleared naturally) = easy vaccine.

subject: Biology
question_text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, mRNA vaccines were deployed at record speed. Explain how mRNA vaccines work and evaluate the factors that enabled rapid development.
option_a: mRNA vaccines contain live COVID-19 virus and work like traditional vaccines
option_b: mRNA vaccines deliver instructions (mRNA coding for spike protein) into cells. Ribosomes translate the mRNA, producing spike protein on cell surfaces. The immune system generates antibodies and memory cells against spike protein, without any viral DNA entering the nucleus or risk of infection. Rapid development: mRNA platform existed (previously tested for other diseases), sequence published immediately, unprecedented funding, parallel Phase II/III trials, emergency use authorisation.
option_c: mRNA vaccines alter human DNA permanently
option_d: mRNA vaccines only provide immunity for one week
explanation: mRNA is translated into antigen protein, stimulating immune response. No integration into DNA (mRNA does not enter nucleus, is rapidly degraded). Speed factors: pre-existing technology, fast sequence-to-vaccine timeline, regulatory flexibility, parallel trials.
correction_tip: mRNA vaccine: mRNA → ribosome → spike protein → immune response. Does NOT enter nucleus, does NOT alter DNA. mRNA degrades within days. Rapid COVID vaccine: mRNA platform pre-existing, sequence published Jan 2020, massive funding, parallel trials. Traditional vaccines: years. Pfizer/Moderna BNT162b2: ~95% efficacy.

subject: Biology
question_text: A patient is given a radioactively labelled monoclonal antibody targeting a specific cancer antigen. Describe how this treatment works and analyse the advantages and limitations compared to external radiotherapy.
option_a: Radioimmunotherapy and external radiotherapy work in identical ways with no differences
option_b: Radioimmunotherapy: antibody seeks and binds specifically to tumour antigen, delivering radiation directly to cancer cells. Advantages: targeted (less normal tissue radiation), can reach metastatic deposits unreachable by external beam. Limitations: not all cancers express specific antigens, antibody may not penetrate large solid tumours, human immune response to mouse antibodies (HAMA), dosing complex. External radiotherapy: can treat larger volumes but causes collateral normal tissue damage.
option_c: Radioimmunotherapy always cures cancer with no limitations
option_d: External radiotherapy is always superior to radioimmunotherapy
explanation: Targeted radiation therapy exploits antibody specificity to deliver a lethal radiation dose to tumour cells. However, solid tumour penetration is limited, antigen expression is required, and radiation dose to individual cells may be lower than external beam. Both have roles depending on cancer type.
correction_tip: Radioimmunotherapy (RIT): antibody-radioisotope conjugate → binds tumour antigen → localised radiation. Good for: haematological cancers (cells in suspension). Limitations: antigen required, poor solid tumour penetration. External radiotherapy: localised beam, larger dose but less specific. HAMA = human anti-mouse antibody response (problem with mouse-derived antibodies).

subject: Biology
question_text: Critically evaluate the use of placebo-controlled trials in testing new antibiotics for antibiotic-resistant infections where few alternatives exist.
option_a: Placebo-controlled trials are always ethically acceptable regardless of the disease severity
option_b: Ethical tension: gold-standard double-blind placebo RCT requires one group receive placebo, acceptable when no effective treatment exists. For serious, life-threatening resistant infections, withholding any treatment from the placebo group may be unethical — risk of death or serious harm. Solution: use active-comparator trials (new drug vs best current treatment), adaptive trial designs (switch patients to effective arm early), or pathogen-specific compassionate use. Regulatory bodies now accept non-inferior active-comparator designs for resistant infections.
option_c: Placebo trials are not used in antibiotic research
option_d: Ethics committees always approve placebo trials regardless of patient risk
explanation: The Declaration of Helsinki requires that patients not be denied effective treatment. For life-threatening resistant infections, active-comparator designs maintain scientific rigour while meeting ethical obligations. Adaptive trials can stop early for efficacy or harm.
correction_tip: Ethics of placebo control: acceptable when no treatment exists; problematic for life-threatening conditions (withholds potentially life-saving treatment). Solutions: active comparator (new vs best available), adaptive design, early stopping rules, compassionate use. MRSA/XDR-TB: active-comparator trials preferred.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain the concept of ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity) and how it bridges innate and adaptive immunity.
option_a: ADCC is a type of antibiotic treatment for bacterial infections
option_b: ADCC occurs when antibodies (adaptive immunity) bind to antigens on infected or cancer cells. The Fc region of the antibody is recognised by Fc receptors on NK cells, macrophages, and neutrophils (innate immunity). This triggers the innate cells to kill the antibody-coated target cell. ADCC bridges adaptive (specific antibody production) and innate (non-specific cytotoxic killing) systems.
option_c: ADCC only operates against bacteria outside cells
option_d: ADCC is only active in newborns before their adaptive immune system develops
explanation: ADCC is important in antiviral and antitumour immunity. Antibodies opsonise targets; NK cells (via CD16/FcγRIII) recognise the Fc region and release cytotoxic granules. Many therapeutic antibodies (e.g. Herceptin) partly work via ADCC.
correction_tip: ADCC: antibody (adaptive) coats target cell → NK cells/macrophages (innate) recognise Fc region → kill cell. Bridges adaptive and innate immunity. Important for: virus-infected cell killing, tumour clearance. Herceptin mechanism includes ADCC. NK cells: innate cytotoxic lymphocytes.

subject: Biology
question_text: Analyse the global public health implications of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), considering the economic, clinical, and preventative dimensions.
option_a: AMR is a minor issue affecting only hospitals in developing countries
option_b: Clinical: resistant infections require longer hospital stays, more expensive drugs, have higher mortality (MRSA, drug-resistant TB kill hundreds of thousands annually; WHO predicts 10 million deaths/year by 2050 if unchecked). Economic: increased treatment costs, lost productivity. Prevention: antibiotic stewardship (prescribe only when necessary, complete courses), surveillance, new drug development (market failure — low profit incentive), vaccines to reduce infection rates, One Health approach (reduce agricultural antibiotic use).
option_c: AMR only affects developing countries and has no global economic impact
option_d: AMR will be solved within 5 years through new antibiotic discovery
explanation: AMR is a global emergency. Current trajectory: 700,000 deaths/year from resistant infections. Without action: 10 million/year by 2050. Market failure in antibiotic development (short courses = low profit). WHO priority pathogens list. Agricultural AMR: 70% of global antibiotics used in livestock.
correction_tip: AMR dimensions: clinical (higher mortality, limited options), economic (10 trillion GDP loss by 2050), prevention (stewardship, new drugs, vaccines, One Health). Key resistant threats: MRSA, CRE, XDR-TB, drug-resistant gonorrhoea. Market failure: low financial incentive for new antibiotic development (short course, low price vs cancer drugs).

subject: Biology
question_text: A new pathogen emerges with a basic reproduction number (R0) of 4. Explain what this means and calculate the herd immunity threshold required to control it.
option_a: R0 = 4 means the pathogen is four times more dangerous than the average disease
option_b: R0 = 4 means each infected person infects 4 others on average in a fully susceptible population. Herd immunity threshold (HIT) = 1 - (1/R0) = 1 - (1/4) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75 = 75%. So 75% of the population must be immune (through vaccination or prior infection) to reduce the effective reproduction number below 1, causing case numbers to decline. Measles R0 ~ 12-18 requires ~94% immunity.
option_c: R0 = 4 means the disease kills 4% of infected individuals
option_d: HIT = R0 × 100% = 400% which is impossible to achieve
explanation: R0 describes transmissibility. HIT = 1 - (1/R0). For R0=4: HIT = 75%. The effective reproduction number Re = R0 × (proportion susceptible). For Re < 1 (epidemic declining), proportion immune must exceed HIT.
correction_tip: R0 = basic reproduction number (infections per case in fully susceptible population). R0 >1: spreading. R0 <1: declining. HIT = 1 - 1/R0. Examples: R0=2 → HIT=50%; R0=4 → HIT=75%; R0=12 (measles) → HIT=92%. Vaccination campaigns target HIT.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain why viruses cannot be treated with antibiotics, and critically evaluate current strategies for treating viral infections.
option_a: Antibiotics treat all infections equally; the pathogen type does not matter
option_b: Viruses have no cell walls, ribosomes, or metabolic pathways of their own — antibiotic targets do not exist in viruses. Viruses hijack host cell machinery, making it hard to target them without also damaging host cells. Current antiviral strategies: (1) inhibit specific viral enzymes (e.g. reverse transcriptase inhibitors for HIV, neuraminidase inhibitors for flu); (2) block viral entry (e.g. HIV fusion inhibitors); (3) vaccines to prevent infection; (4) interferons to boost innate antiviral defences. All target virus-specific features.
option_c: Viruses can be treated with low doses of antibiotics that are too weak to affect the body
option_d: Antivirals work by killing viruses in the same way antibiotics kill bacteria
explanation: Virus-specific drug targets: reverse transcriptase (HIV, HBV), neuraminidase (influenza), protease (HIV, HCV), integrase (HIV). Selective toxicity requires targeting viral proteins not found in host cells. Intracellular replication makes this challenging.
correction_tip: No antibiotic targets in viruses: no cell wall (no penicillin target), no 70S ribosomes (no tetracycline target), use host cell machinery. Antivirals target virus-specific enzymes: neuraminidase inhibitors (Tamiflu), reverse transcriptase inhibitors (AZT for HIV), protease inhibitors (HIV, HCV). Vaccines = best strategy.

subject: Biology
question_text: Evaluate the use of monoclonal antibodies in treating autoimmune conditions, using rheumatoid arthritis as an example.
option_a: Monoclonal antibodies cannot treat autoimmune conditions as they would attack the body
option_b: In rheumatoid arthritis, TNF-alpha (tumour necrosis factor) drives inflammatory joint destruction. Anti-TNF monoclonal antibodies (e.g. infliximab/Remicade, adalimumab/Humira) bind and neutralise TNF-alpha, reducing joint inflammation. Benefits: highly effective for TNF-driven disease, specific mechanism. Limitations: expensive (~£10,000/year), increased infection risk (TNF is also important for fighting infection), some patients develop antibodies against the treatment (loss of efficacy), not effective for all patients.
option_c: Monoclonal antibody treatment for arthritis is still purely experimental
option_d: Anti-TNF drugs treat autoimmune diseases by replacing the damaged joints
explanation: Biologics (monoclonal antibodies targeting inflammatory mediators) revolutionised treatment of autoimmune diseases. Anti-TNF drugs: block TNF-α (key inflammatory cytokine) → reduced inflammation in RA, Crohn's, psoriasis. Side effect: immunosuppression (TNF also fights TB).
correction_tip: Anti-TNF biologics: infliximab (chimeric antibody), adalimumab (fully human antibody). Target TNF-alpha (key inflammatory cytokine). Conditions: RA, Crohn's, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis. Side effects: serious infections (TB reactivation risk), cost. Screen for latent TB before starting.

subject: Biology
question_text: A researcher studies a new bacterium with a very thick capsule surrounding its cell wall. Predict how this would affect its interaction with the immune system and its virulence.
option_a: A thick capsule would make the bacterium easier for phagocytes to engulf
option_b: The polysaccharide capsule is a major virulence factor: (1) prevents opsonisation — phagocytes cannot easily bind and engulf encapsulated bacteria; (2) resists complement activation on the bacterial surface; (3) may shield surface antigens from antibody recognition. Encapsulated bacteria (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae) are typically more virulent and cause serious invasive infections. Vaccines targeting capsule polysaccharides (conjugate vaccines) are very effective.
option_c: Bacterial capsules have no effect on immune response
option_d: A thick capsule helps the immune system identify and kill the bacteria more quickly
explanation: Capsule is a classic virulence factor. Without opsonins (antibodies/complement) coating the bacteria, phagocytes cannot effectively engulf them. Capsule polysaccharide vaccines (e.g. pneumococcal PCV13, meningococcal vaccine) generate anti-capsule antibodies to overcome this.
correction_tip: Bacterial capsule virulence: resists phagocytosis (no handles for phagocyte receptors), inhibits complement, shields from antibodies. Examples: S. pneumoniae (pneumonia/meningitis), N. meningitidis (meningitis), Hib (meningitis). Conjugate vaccines: capsule polysaccharide + carrier protein → T-cell help → strong immunity.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain the concept of "original antigenic sin" (immunological imprinting) and its significance for influenza vaccine effectiveness in different age groups.
option_a: Original antigenic sin means the immune system can only respond to one antigen ever
option_b: Original antigenic sin: the immune system preferentially recalls B-cells from the first influenza infection encountered in childhood, even when exposed to a different variant later. These original memory cells dominate the response, potentially producing antibodies less well-matched to the current circulating strain. This means individuals may respond less optimally to flu vaccines if the vaccine strain differs from their "imprinted" strain. Has implications for pandemic preparedness and why vaccine effectiveness varies by birth year.
option_c: Original antigenic sin means elderly people cannot be vaccinated against flu
option_d: Original antigenic sin refers to antibiotics becoming ineffective over time
explanation: First influenza infection shapes lifelong immune responses. Birth year correlates with which historical flu strains shaped immune memory. 2009 pandemic H1N1 paradoxically had lower mortality in elderly people — their immune imprinting from 1918-like strains provided cross-protection.
correction_tip: Original antigenic sin/immunological imprinting: first flu infection establishes dominant memory. Later exposures recall original memory even if suboptimal. 2009 H1N1: older adults (born pre-1957) had better protection from H1 imprinting. Implications: vaccine design, pandemic preparedness, explains why flu vaccine effectiveness varies by age cohort.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
option_a: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
option_b: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy)
option_c: Glucose + water → carbon dioxide + ATP + heat
option_d: Oxygen + carbon dioxide → glucose + water
explanation: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. This requires light energy (usually from sunlight) and takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells.
correction_tip: Photosynthesis: CO2 + H2O → C6H12O6 + O2 (light energy). Respiration is the reverse. Remember: photosynthesis makes glucose (stores energy); respiration releases it.

subject: Biology
question_text: Where in a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
option_a: Mitochondria
option_b: Nucleus
option_c: Chloroplasts
option_d: Vacuole
explanation: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts. Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll which absorbs light energy.
correction_tip: Chloroplasts: photosynthesis. Contain chlorophyll (absorbs light). Mitochondria: respiration. Both organelles have double membranes and their own DNA (endosymbiotic origin).

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
option_a: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
option_b: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP)
option_c: Glucose → lactic acid + energy
option_d: Glucose + water → carbon dioxide + ATP
explanation: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP. This takes place in the mitochondria and releases the most energy from glucose.
correction_tip: Aerobic respiration: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP. Mitochondria. Anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid (animals) or ethanol + CO2 (plants/yeast). Aerobic releases ~38 ATP per glucose; anaerobic ~2 ATP.

subject: Biology
question_text: What happens to glucose that is produced by photosynthesis in a plant?
option_a: It is immediately released into the air as carbon dioxide
option_b: It can be used for respiration, converted to starch for storage, used to make cellulose cell walls, or used to make proteins and fats
option_c: It is only used to make more chlorophyll
option_d: It is all excreted through the roots
explanation: Glucose from photosynthesis is used for: respiration (energy), converted to starch (storage), cellulose (cell walls), sucrose (transport), fats, and with nitrogen, proteins.
correction_tip: Glucose uses: respiration (energy), starch (storage in leaves/seeds), cellulose (cell wall), sucrose (transport in phloem), lipids (storage), + nitrates → amino acids → proteins.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
option_a: To store glucose produced by photosynthesis
option_b: To absorb light energy for use in photosynthesis
option_c: To carry oxygen out of the leaf
option_d: To absorb carbon dioxide from the air
explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy (mainly red and blue wavelengths, reflecting green which is why plants appear green). This energy drives photosynthesis.
correction_tip: Chlorophyll: absorbs red and blue light, reflects green. Light energy → chemical energy (ATP + NADPH) → used to fix CO2 into glucose. No chlorophyll → no photosynthesis. Different pigments absorb different wavelengths.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is anaerobic respiration in animals?
option_a: Respiration using oxygen in the mitochondria
option_b: Respiration without oxygen that converts glucose to lactic acid, releasing a small amount of energy
option_c: Respiration that converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide
option_d: Respiration that only occurs in plants
explanation: Animal anaerobic respiration: glucose → lactic acid + energy (ATP). Less energy than aerobic. Occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient (e.g. vigorous exercise). Lactic acid causes muscle fatigue.
correction_tip: Animal anaerobic: glucose → lactic acid + ATP (small amount). Yeast/plant anaerobic: glucose → ethanol + CO2 + ATP. Both: no O2 required, less ATP than aerobic. Lactic acid → oxygen debt (repaid after exercise stops).

subject: Biology
question_text: Name three factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
option_a: Temperature, water availability, and light intensity only
option_b: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, and temperature
option_c: Oxygen concentration, sugar concentration, and rainfall
option_d: Soil minerals, oxygen levels, and leaf colour
explanation: The three main limiting factors for photosynthesis are: light intensity (drives light reactions), CO2 concentration (raw material), and temperature (affects enzyme activity). Whichever is lowest limits the rate.
correction_tip: Limiting factors: light intensity, CO2 concentration, temperature. At low light → rate limited by light. At high light + low CO2 → CO2 is limiting. At very high temperatures → enzymes denature → rate falls. On a graph: rate plateaus when another factor becomes limiting.

subject: Biology
question_text: What gas is produced as a by-product of photosynthesis?
option_a: Carbon dioxide
option_b: Nitrogen
option_c: Oxygen
option_d: Water vapour
explanation: Oxygen is released as a by-product of photosynthesis. It is produced when water molecules are split by light energy (photolysis of water) during the light-dependent reactions.
correction_tip: Photosynthesis: CO2 + H2O → glucose + O2. Oxygen = by-product from water splitting (photolysis). Oxygen is the raw material of aerobic respiration. All atmospheric oxygen comes from photosynthesis.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why do plants need mineral ions as well as carbon dioxide and water?
option_a: Mineral ions are needed as a source of energy for photosynthesis
option_b: Minerals are needed to make other biological molecules: nitrates for amino acids and proteins, magnesium for chlorophyll, phosphates for DNA and ATP
option_c: Minerals replace water as the hydrogen source for photosynthesis
option_d: Minerals are only needed for root growth and have no role in leaves
explanation: Plants cannot make all molecules from CO2 and H2O alone. Nitrates (NO3⁻) provide nitrogen for amino acids and proteins; magnesium (Mg²⁺) is needed for chlorophyll synthesis; phosphates for DNA and ATP.
correction_tip: Mineral ions: nitrates → amino acids (N needed). Magnesium → chlorophyll (Mg core). Phosphates → DNA, ATP, cell membrane. Deficiencies: no nitrates → yellowing (chlorosis) from reduced chlorophyll. No Mg → chlorophyll cannot be made.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is meant by the compensation point in plants?
option_a: The temperature at which photosynthesis stops
option_b: The light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis exactly equals the rate of respiration — the net gas exchange is zero
option_c: The point at which a plant has made enough glucose for the day
option_d: The point at which all oxygen produced by photosynthesis is used in respiration
explanation: At the compensation point, CO2 produced by respiration equals CO2 absorbed by photosynthesis, and O2 produced equals O2 consumed. At higher light intensities, photosynthesis exceeds respiration and the plant makes a net gain.
correction_tip: Compensation point: photosynthesis rate = respiration rate. Net gas exchange = zero. Below: respiration > photosynthesis (plant uses stored food). Above: photosynthesis > respiration (net gain of glucose). Important for understanding plant growth in different light conditions.

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the main use of ATP in cells?
option_a: ATP is used as the main building block for DNA
option_b: ATP provides immediate energy for cell processes including active transport, muscle contraction, protein synthesis, and cell division
option_c: ATP stores energy permanently for future use
option_d: ATP is only used in plant cells during photosynthesis
explanation: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the universal energy currency of cells. It transfers energy from respiration to processes that need it. When ATP is hydrolysed to ADP + phosphate, energy is released for cellular work.
correction_tip: ATP: universal energy currency. Made in respiration, used for: active transport, muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, nerve impulses. ATP → ADP + Pi + energy (hydrolysis). ADP + Pi → ATP (in respiration). Not stored long-term.

subject: Biology
question_text: Which leaf feature allows gas exchange for photosynthesis?
option_a: The waxy cuticle on the upper surface
option_b: Stomata — tiny pores on the leaf surface (mainly the underside) that allow CO2 to enter and O2 to exit
option_c: The veins (vascular bundles) that carry gases around the leaf
option_d: Chlorophyll molecules that attract CO2 directly
explanation: Stomata are pores bordered by guard cells. During the day, guard cells absorb water and swell, opening the stomata to allow CO2 in and O2 out. They close at night or when water is scarce.
correction_tip: Stomata: CO2 in, O2 out (photosynthesis); O2 in, CO2 out (respiration); water vapour out (transpiration). Guard cells control opening/closing. Most on underside of leaf (shaded, cooler, reduces water loss).

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain why increasing CO2 concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis, up to a point.
option_a: More CO2 provides more energy for the light reactions
option_b: CO2 is a raw material in the Calvin cycle (dark reactions). More CO2 increases the rate of carbon fixation (RuBisCO enzyme activity), increasing glucose production. However, at some point another factor (light or temperature) becomes limiting and the rate plateaus.
option_c: CO2 prevents chlorophyll from breaking down so it can absorb more light
option_d: CO2 opens stomata wider increasing gas exchange
explanation: CO2 is fixed into organic molecules (glucose) in the Calvin cycle by the enzyme RuBisCO. More CO2 = more substrate for this enzyme = faster carbon fixation until another factor limits the rate.
correction_tip: CO2: raw material for Calvin cycle (dark reactions). Rate ↑ with [CO2] until another factor limits. Light reactions produce ATP/NADPH used in Calvin cycle. CO2 + RuBP (5C) → RuBisCO → 2× GP (3C) → G3P → glucose.

subject: Biology
question_text: A plant kept at 35°C showed a decreased rate of photosynthesis compared to 25°C, despite adequate light and CO2. Explain this observation.
option_a: High temperature improves enzyme activity so the rate should have increased
option_b: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled (RuBisCO and other Calvin cycle enzymes). At 35°C, enzymes begin to lose their optimal shape — some denaturation occurs, reducing the rate. Also, stomata may close at high temperatures to prevent water loss, reducing CO2 entry.
option_c: High temperature converts chlorophyll to a different pigment that cannot absorb light
option_d: The glucose produced at 25°C cannot be made at 35°C
explanation: Above optimal temperature (~25°C for many plants), enzyme denaturation begins reducing photosynthetic rate. Additionally, high temperature increases transpiration risk, causing stomata to close, reducing CO2 entry and further limiting photosynthesis.
correction_tip: Temperature and photosynthesis: ↑temp → ↑rate (to optimum) → above optimum → enzymes denature → ↓rate. Also: high temp → stomata close (prevent water loss) → ↓CO2 → ↓rate. Typical optimum ~25-30°C. Different from high temp meaning enzymes are totally denatured.

subject: Biology
question_text: During intense exercise, why do muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration?
option_a: Muscles prefer anaerobic respiration because it produces more ATP
option_b: During intense exercise, muscles demand more oxygen than the circulatory system can supply. When oxygen runs out in muscles, aerobic respiration cannot continue. Anaerobic respiration (glucose → lactic acid) provides a small amount of ATP rapidly to keep muscles working, albeit less efficiently.
option_c: Muscle cells do not have mitochondria so always use anaerobic respiration
option_d: Anaerobic respiration is triggered when body temperature rises above 37°C
explanation: Oxygen delivery to muscles is rate-limited by heart rate and blood flow. When demand exceeds supply, the limited oxygen is quickly used up. Anaerobic glycolysis continues ATP production without oxygen, but less efficiently.
correction_tip: Exercise oxygen demand > supply → anaerobic respiration. Glucose → lactic acid + 2 ATP (instead of ~38 ATP aerobically). Lactic acid = muscle fatigue, cramp. After exercise: oxygen debt repaid (liver converts lactic acid back to glucose).

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain what happens to lactic acid produced during anaerobic respiration after exercise stops.
option_a: Lactic acid is permanently stored in the muscles
option_b: After exercise, the person continues to breathe heavily (oxygen debt). The extra oxygen oxidises lactic acid: it is transported to the liver where it is converted back to glucose (gluconeogenesis). The faster heart rate and breathing help clear lactic acid from muscles, relieving the cramp.
option_c: Lactic acid evaporates through the skin as sweat
option_d: Lactic acid is converted directly to CO2 and exhaled
explanation: Oxygen debt (EPOC): the extra oxygen needed after exercise to metabolise accumulated lactic acid. Liver converts lactic acid to pyruvate and then to glucose (energy required). This is why breathing rate remains elevated after exercise stops.
correction_tip: Lactic acid → liver → gluconeogenesis (lactic acid → glucose). Requires O2 → explains "oxygen debt" (now called EPOC). Heavy breathing after exercise = repaying oxygen debt. Heart rate stays elevated to transport lactic acid to liver quickly.

subject: Biology
question_text: How are leaves adapted for photosynthesis?
option_a: Leaves are thick with few pores to retain water
option_b: Leaves are thin (short diffusion distance), flat (large SA for light absorption), have a transparent cuticle (light passes through), stomata (gas exchange), palisade cells near upper surface (packed with chloroplasts), veins (water and mineral supply, glucose export).
option_c: Leaves are adapted only to prevent water loss and have no role in photosynthesis
option_d: Leaves have one cell type that performs all leaf functions
explanation: Leaf adaptations: large flat surface (maximum light absorption), thin (short diffusion path for gases), palisade layer (densely packed chloroplasts), stomata (CO2/O2 exchange), spongy mesophyll (air spaces for gas diffusion), veins (water supply, glucose removal).
correction_tip: Leaf adaptations: flat+large (SA for light), thin (↓diffusion distance), transparent cuticle (light reaches palisade), palisade cells upper (most light, most chloroplasts), stomata (CO2 in, O2 out), spongy layer (air spaces), veins (water in, glucose out).

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the effect of increasing light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis, and why does it plateau?
option_a: Rate continues to increase indefinitely as light intensity increases
option_b: As light intensity increases, photosynthesis rate increases proportionally (more energy for light reactions). Eventually the rate plateaus because CO2 concentration or temperature becomes the limiting factor — additional light cannot further increase the rate.
option_c: Rate decreases at high light intensities because the plant is damaged
option_d: Light intensity has no effect on photosynthesis — only CO2 matters
explanation: Light drives the light-dependent reactions (splitting water, producing ATP and NADPH). More light = faster rate. But at some point, the rate is limited by CO2 supply or enzyme activity (temperature-dependent), causing a plateau on the rate vs light intensity graph.
correction_tip: Light intensity vs rate: linear increase then plateau. Plateau = another factor is limiting (CO2 or temperature). To confirm: increase CO2 → plateau shifts up. This is a standard exam graph — be able to identify the limiting factor from the plateau.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe how gardeners can use knowledge of limiting factors to maximise crop yield in a greenhouse.
option_a: Gardeners should reduce all factors to minimise photosynthesis and slow growth
option_b: Increase CO2 levels (paraffin heaters produce CO2, or add CO2 tanks), maintain optimal temperature (25-30°C), use supplementary artificial lighting in winter or at night, and ensure adequate water and nutrients. This eliminates limiting factors so photosynthesis runs at maximum rate year-round.
option_c: Greenhouses are used only to protect plants from frost, not to increase photosynthesis
option_d: Increasing just one factor is always sufficient to maximise yield
explanation: Greenhouses can control all limiting factors simultaneously: light (supplementary lamps), CO2 (added from heaters or gas), temperature (heating), water (irrigation). Removing all limiting factors maximises photosynthesis and therefore yield.
correction_tip: Greenhouse control: CO2 enrichment (burning paraffin/gas adds CO2), supplementary lighting (LEDs), temperature control (heating). All factors must be optimised — removing one limit means another limit takes over. Commercial greenhouses routinely use CO2 enrichment.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why does fermentation in yeast produce ethanol and CO2 rather than lactic acid?
option_a: Yeast is unable to produce lactic acid due to its eukaryotic nature
option_b: Yeast uses a different anaerobic pathway from animal cells: glucose → ethanol + CO2 + ATP. The enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase converts pyruvate differently from the lactate dehydrogenase enzyme in animal muscle cells.
option_c: Ethanol production requires oxygen; lactic acid does not
option_d: Yeast has no mitochondria so always produces ethanol
explanation: Both animal and yeast anaerobic respiration regenerate NAD⁺ needed for glycolysis to continue, but use different terminal electron acceptors: animals use pyruvate (→ lactic acid); yeast/plants use pyruvate via different route (→ ethanol + CO2).
correction_tip: Yeast anaerobic: glucose → pyruvate → ethanol + CO2. Animal anaerobic: glucose → pyruvate → lactic acid. Both regenerate NAD+ for glycolysis. Yeast fermentation used in bread (CO2 bubbles), beer/wine (ethanol). Both: less ATP than aerobic.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe the three main factors affecting metabolic rate and oxygen consumption in humans.
option_a: Only body size affects metabolic rate; other factors are unimportant
option_b: (1) Exercise/activity level: muscle contraction requires ATP from respiration, greatly increasing O2 consumption. (2) Thermoregulation: maintaining body temperature in cold conditions requires more respiration to generate heat. (3) Body size: larger organisms have higher total metabolic rate (but smaller surface area to volume ratio means less heat loss per kg).
option_c: Metabolic rate is constant for all humans regardless of activity or temperature
option_d: Only food intake affects metabolic rate; no other factors matter
explanation: Metabolic rate determines oxygen consumption. Exercise is the most variable factor. Thermogenesis in cold environments increases resting metabolic rate. Larger body mass means more total cells respiring, but metabolic rate per kilogram is lower.
correction_tip: Metabolic rate factors: exercise (↑ ATP demand → ↑ respiration), temperature (cold → shivering thermogenesis → ↑ respiration), body size (more cells = more total respiration). Measured as O2 consumption rate. BMR = basal metabolic rate (at rest, warm).

subject: Biology
question_text: A student investigates photosynthesis using Canadian pondweed (Elodea) and counts oxygen bubbles. The student moves a lamp closer and the bubble rate increases. What variable is being changed and what should be controlled?
option_a: Changing CO2 concentration; controlling light intensity
option_b: Changing light intensity (closer lamp = more light per unit area); controlling temperature (use water bath), CO2 concentration (add fixed amount of sodium bicarbonate), species and mass of pondweed, time counted.
option_c: Changing temperature; controlling oxygen levels
option_d: Changing water temperature only; nothing else needs controlling
explanation: Moving the lamp changes light intensity (intensity ∝ 1/distance²). To make it a fair test: temperature must be controlled (water bath prevents lamp heating the water), CO2 must be constant (add sodium bicarbonate solution), and pondweed mass/species must be identical.
correction_tip: Pondweed photosynthesis experiment: independent variable = light intensity (lamp distance). Dependent variable = bubble rate (or volume O2). Controls: temperature (water bath), CO2 (sodium bicarbonate), pondweed mass, time. Light intensity ∝ 1/d². Improve: use oxygen sensor.

subject: Biology
question_text: Why does the rate of respiration increase during exercise and how is this coordinated with increased breathing?
option_a: Respiration rate stays constant during exercise; only heart rate changes
option_b: Exercising muscles need more ATP → increased aerobic respiration → more O2 needed and more CO2 produced. Rising CO2 in blood is detected by chemoreceptors, signalling the respiratory centre to increase breathing rate and depth. Increased heart rate delivers O2 faster and removes CO2. Both responses are proportional to exercise intensity.
option_c: Muscles switch entirely to anaerobic respiration during all exercise
option_d: The nervous system directly controls respiration in muscle cells during exercise
explanation: Exercise → increased ATP demand → aerobic respiration increases → O2 consumed and CO2 produced faster. CO2 rise detected by chemoreceptors → increased ventilation rate. Cardiac output also increases. This forms a homeostatic feedback loop.
correction_tip: Exercise → ↑CO2 and ↓pH in blood → chemoreceptors (carotid, medulla) detect → ↑breathing rate+depth. Also ↑heart rate via sympathetic nervous system + adrenaline. Proportional response. CO2 is the primary stimulus for breathing rate change (not O2 usually).

subject: Biology
question_text: What is the action spectrum of photosynthesis and why does it match the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll?
option_a: The action spectrum shows that green light drives most photosynthesis
option_b: The action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths — it peaks in red and blue light, matching the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll (which absorbs red and blue, reflecting green). Wavelengths absorbed by chlorophyll drive photosynthesis; green light is reflected so cannot be absorbed.
option_c: The action spectrum is identical to white light and shows all wavelengths are equally effective
option_d: Chlorophyll absorbs only green light, which explains why plants are green
explanation: Action spectrum: photosynthesis rate vs wavelength — peaks at ~450 nm (blue) and ~680 nm (red). Absorption spectrum of chlorophyll: also peaks at blue and red. Match confirms it is chlorophyll absorbing light that drives photosynthesis. Low activity at green (~550 nm) as chlorophyll reflects it.
correction_tip: Action spectrum ≈ absorption spectrum of chlorophyll. Both peak at blue (~450 nm) and red (~680 nm). Green light (~550 nm): reflected, not absorbed, lowest photosynthesis rate. Multiple pigments (carotenoids) extend absorption range. This is evidence that chlorophyll drives photosynthesis.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain the two main stages of photosynthesis and where they occur within the chloroplast.
option_a: Photosynthesis has only one stage that occurs in the stroma
option_b: Stage 1 — Light-dependent reactions (thylakoid membranes): light splits water (photolysis), producing O2, ATP, and NADPH. Stage 2 — Light-independent reactions/Calvin cycle (stroma): ATP and NADPH are used to fix CO2 into G3P and eventually glucose. The thylakoid stacking (grana) maximises SA for light reactions; stroma is the fluid matrix for the Calvin cycle.
option_c: Stage 1 occurs in the stroma; stage 2 occurs on the thylakoid membrane
option_d: Both stages occur in the outer membrane of the chloroplast
explanation: Thylakoid membranes: light reactions — chlorophyll absorbs light, photolysis of water produces O2, ATP synthesised by photophosphorylation, NADPH produced. Stroma: Calvin cycle — CO2 fixed by RuBisCO into 3-carbon molecules (GP), reduced using ATP+NADPH to G3P → glucose.
correction_tip: Light-dependent (thylakoid): light → ATP + NADPH, water → O2 (photolysis). Light-independent/Calvin cycle (stroma): CO2 + RuBP → RuBisCO → GP → G3P → glucose (uses ATP+NADPH). Thylakoid = grana (stacked membranes). Stroma = fluid surrounding grana.

subject: Biology
question_text: A plant experiment shows that at high light intensities, increasing CO2 from 0.04% to 0.1% increases the photosynthesis rate significantly, but at low light intensities, the same CO2 increase has little effect. Explain these results.
option_a: CO2 only affects photosynthesis at low light intensities
option_b: At low light intensity, light is the limiting factor — the light-dependent reactions produce insufficient ATP and NADPH regardless of CO2 supply. More CO2 cannot help if the Calvin cycle lacks energy. At high light intensity, light is no longer limiting and CO2 becomes the limiting factor; increasing it allows more carbon fixation and higher rates.
option_c: High light intensity makes plants insensitive to CO2 changes permanently
option_d: CO2 affects only the light-dependent reactions so is only relevant at high light
explanation: When light is limiting (low intensity), the Calvin cycle is starved of ATP/NADPH regardless of CO2. When light is sufficient (high intensity), CO2 supply becomes limiting. This illustrates Blackman's law of limiting factors: the factor in shortest supply limits the overall rate.
correction_tip: Blackman's law: rate limited by factor in least supply. Low light → light limits → ↑CO2 no help. High light → CO2 limits → ↑CO2 increases rate. Identifying limiting factors: the factor whose increase still increases rate is the current limiting factor.

subject: Biology
question_text: Describe the full process of aerobic respiration, including where each stage occurs in the cell.
option_a: Aerobic respiration occurs entirely in the cytoplasm with no role for mitochondria
option_b: Stage 1 — Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (3C) + 2 ATP + 2 NADH. Stage 2 — Link reaction (mitochondrial matrix): pyruvate → acetyl CoA (2C) + CO2 + NADH. Stage 3 — Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix): acetyl CoA enters, producing CO2, NADH, FADH2, and 2 ATP per cycle. Stage 4 — Oxidative phosphorylation (inner mitochondrial membrane): electron carriers use H from NADH/FADH2 with O2 → water + ~34 ATP.
option_c: Aerobic respiration only occurs in the matrix of the mitochondria
option_d: Glucose is directly converted to CO2 and water in one step in the cytoplasm
explanation: Full aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm) → pyruvate; link reaction (matrix) → acetyl CoA; Krebs cycle (matrix) → CO2, reduced carriers; oxidative phosphorylation (inner membrane) → 34 ATP from electron transport chain. Total: ~38 ATP per glucose.
correction_tip: Aerobic stages: 1) Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose→pyruvate, 2ATP. 2) Link reaction (matrix): pyruvate→acetyl CoA, CO2. 3) Krebs (matrix): 2 ATP, CO2, NADH, FADH2. 4) Oxidative phosphorylation (inner membrane): ~34 ATP, H2O. GCSE simplified: glucose+O2→CO2+H2O+ATP.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain why a plant kept in complete darkness for several days would eventually die, using your knowledge of bioenergetics.
option_a: Plants die in darkness only because they cannot make water
option_b: Without light, photosynthesis stops completely. The plant must rely on stored starch and glucose for respiration. As stores are depleted, the plant cannot: synthesise new proteins, lipids, or cellulose (no glucose substrate); generate ATP for active transport of minerals; maintain cell structure. Eventually starvation leads to cell death. However, the plant continues to respire using stored reserves.
option_c: Plants cannot respire so they die instantly without light
option_d: Darkness stops both photosynthesis and respiration simultaneously
explanation: Plants do not stop respiring in darkness — they use stored glucose/starch. Without photosynthesis replenishing glucose, stores deplete. Active processes (mineral uptake, cell repair, growth) all require ATP from glucose. Complete glucose depletion is fatal.
correction_tip: Dark: photosynthesis = 0, respiration continues (using stored food). Below compensation point: respiration > photosynthesis. Long darkness → stored glucose depleted → starvation. Plants don't stop respiring in dark. Evidence: plants in dark produce CO2 and consume O2.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain why sprint athletes experience oxygen debt (EPOC) and describe the physiological processes involved in recovery.
option_a: Oxygen debt occurs because the lungs close during sprinting
option_b: During sprinting, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid faster than it can be removed. After stopping, the body needs extra oxygen beyond normal resting levels (EPOC = excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) to: (1) oxidise lactic acid in the liver to pyruvate, then to CO2/H2O or glucose; (2) restore ATP and phosphocreatine reserves; (3) return O2 levels to normal in blood and muscles. This explains why breathing remains elevated for minutes after sprinting.
option_c: Oxygen debt means the body borrowed oxygen from its fat stores
option_d: EPOC only occurs in untrained athletes and disappears with regular training
explanation: EPOC: O2 used post-exercise to process accumulated lactic acid and restore energy stores. Liver reconverts lactic acid to glucose via gluconeogenesis (requires ATP from aerobic respiration). Phosphocreatine is resynthesised. Elevated heart and breathing rates help deliver extra O2.
correction_tip: EPOC: extra O2 after exercise. Processes: 1) Lactic acid → pyruvate → glucose (liver gluconeogenesis), 2) Restore PCr (phosphocreatine), 3) Restore O2 in blood/muscle. Explains heavy breathing after exercise. Magnitude ∝ exercise intensity and duration.

subject: Biology
question_text: Calculate: a plant produces 200 µmol of O2 per hour by photosynthesis and uses 50 µmol of O2 per hour for its own respiration. What is the net O2 output per hour and what is the gross photosynthesis rate?
option_a: Net = 200 µmol; gross = 150 µmol
option_b: Net O2 output = 200 - 50 = 150 µmol/hour (apparent/net photosynthesis). Gross photosynthesis = 200 µmol/hour (total O2 produced before any is used in respiration). The 50 µmol used in respiration is not released to the surroundings.
option_c: Net = 50 µmol; gross = 200 µmol
option_d: Net = 250 µmol; gross = 200 µmol
explanation: Gross photosynthesis = total O2 produced = 200 µmol/h. Net photosynthesis (apparent) = gross - respiration = 200 - 50 = 150 µmol/h (what you can actually measure from outside the plant). Gross = net + respiration.
correction_tip: Gross photosynthesis = total O2 produced. Net photosynthesis = gross - respiration. Measurements: only net can be measured (net gas exchange). Gross = net + respiration rate. At compensation point: gross PS = respiration, net = 0. Standard exam calculation.

subject: Biology
question_text: Explain how the structure of the mitochondrion is adapted for its role in aerobic respiration.
option_a: Mitochondria are smooth spheres with no internal membranes
option_b: Outer membrane: allows small molecules in. Inner membrane: highly folded into cristae — dramatically increasing surface area for electron transport chain enzymes and ATP synthase. Matrix: contains enzymes for Krebs cycle and link reaction, circular DNA, and ribosomes. Many mitochondria in active cells (muscle cells) as each produces ATP.
option_c: Mitochondria have no internal structure — ATP is made at the outer surface
option_d: The folded inner membrane stores glucose for immediate respiration
explanation: Cristae: folded inner membrane greatly increases SA for electron transport chain (ETC) and ATP synthase. Matrix: site of Krebs cycle and link reaction enzymes. Intermembrane space: H⁺ gradient for chemiosmosis. Double membrane: outer (smooth), inner (cristae).
